body:
Release PR for the Go module, the counterpart to the release-plz PR for the
crates and the `release-ts` PR for the npm package. **Merging this is the
release**: the `publish-go` job in `publish.yml` sees a `Version` that has
no matching tag and pushes `trust-tasks-go/v0.1.2`, after which
`proxy.golang.org` serves it and `go get github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go@v0.1.2` resolves.

- `github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go`: `0.1.1` → `0.1.2` (`patch`)
- derived from the conventional commits in `trust-tasks-go/v0.1.1..HEAD` touching `specs/`,
  `trust-tasks-go/` or `scripts/build-go-bindings.mjs`

There is no registry account and no token involved — a Go module is published
by tagging a public repository.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(dart-tsp): TSP transport binding for Dart (trust_tasks_tsp)
body:
Adds **`trust_tasks_tsp`**, the ToIP Trust Spanning Protocol transport binding (`bindings/tsp/0.1`) for Dart, built on Affinidi's [`affinidi-tsp-dart`](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tsp-dart). The Dart counterpart of the Rust `trust-tasks-tsp` crate.

## ⚠️ Cannot be published yet
`affinidi_tsp` is **not on pub.dev** (404), so this package cannot be published either — pub.dev requires every dependency in the published closure to be hosted. It is therefore:
- built and tested against `affinidi_tsp` via a **pinned git override** (`pubspec_overrides.yaml`, commit `5b1cb00`), with the committed `pubspec.yaml` naming the hosted `affinidi_tsp: ^0.1.0` it will resolve against once published;
- **deliberately left out of the release matrices** (`tag-dart`, `release-dart-pr`, `publish-dart.yml`, `release-dart-pr.sh`) — a release deletes the override and `dart pub get` would fail on the unpublished dependency;
- tested by a new `dart.yml` job; `check-dart-packages` permits a tested-but-unreleased package.

**When `affinidi_tsp` publishes:** drop the git override, add the four release entries, flip the website matrix cell, and do the manual first publish. RELEASING.md and CLAUDE.md spell this out.

## Envelope layer
- **`packTrustTask`** seals a **Direct** TSP message (HPKE authenticated encryption + signature). The payload is the envelope object `{"type": envelopeType, "document": <doc>}` — byte-for-byte the shape the Rust crate seals, pinned by a test. A TSP VID **is** a framework VID, so nothing is transformed.
- **`unpackTrustTask`** opens a message under a resolved sender VID, requires it to be sealed (a signed-only message is refused), checks the envelope type, and returns the document plus the authenticated sender.
- Envelope-layer failures throw a typed `TspEnvelopeException` (`notForThisReceiver`, `senderNotAllowed`, `notSealed`, `notFinalRecipient`, `wrongEnvelopeType`, `invalidBody`). None can be answered — TSP has no anonymous sender (§4).

## Consumer: `TspConsumer`
- Reads the message's named sender, checks the allowlist, resolves the sender, opens the sealed message, then runs `consumeInbound`.
- Duplicate-execution record on by default, keyed on the document `id` (§7.1): a re-forward of the same document is absorbed with the first response; a different document under the same `id` is `idConflict`; a store that can't be consulted fails closed with `unavailable`; a handler exception releases the claim.
- An authenticated body that doesn't deserialise is answered `malformedRequest`; an in-band `issuer` that isn't the authenticated sender is `identityMismatch`, sealed back to the sender.
- Proofs verified over the document as received; with no verifier, a proof-bearing document is refused rather than ignored (proof MAY be omitted in Direct/nested mode, §5.3).
- `packReply` seals the reply back to the authenticated sender.

## Scope
This release carries **Direct** messages, the strongest case (§5.1). Routed/nested relaying is the mediator's job on the wire; a layer this VID only relays surfaces as `notFinalRecipient`.

## Interop
- The sealed envelope object matches the Rust `trust-tasks-tsp` crate's `{type, document}` shape exactly — a test opens a Dart seal and asserts the two-key object.
- Cross-implementation TSP **wire** interop rests on the shared TSP Rev 3 conformance vectors that `affinidi_tsp`, `affinidi-tsp-go` and the `affinidi-tsp` Rust crate each test against; it is a property of those libraries, not of this binding, which only adds the envelope object and the §7.2 pipeline.

## Tests
24: Direct round trip, the envelope-shape pin, confidentiality, wrong receiver, wrong sender VID, tamper, signed-only, foreign type, invalid body, no-encryption-key; and the consumer — identity omitted and TSP-supplied, reply round trip, re-forward absorbed, conflict, identity mismatch, recipient mismatch, allowlist, staleness, proof without verifier, malformed payload, handler exception, store failing closed, fire-and-forget. Passes on Dart 3.8 and stable, and analyzes clean on the ssi lower bound.

## A note on TSP keys
`affinidi_tsp` signs with Ed25519 only (the HPKE key agreement is derived from it), so VIDs are built from Ed25519 keys.

## pana
Not meaningfully scorable yet: pana can't resolve the git dependency, so its analysis/platform/dependency checks fail (40/160). The code passes `dart analyze --fatal-infos` and all 24 tests. Once `affinidi_tsp` is on pub.dev and the override is dropped, it should score like the other bindings.

title: feat(go-tsp): TSP transport binding for Go (trust-tasks-go/tsp)
body:
Adds the **ToIP Trust Spanning Protocol (TSP) transport binding for Go**, as a **separate nested module** `trust-tasks-go/tsp`, built on [`github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tsp-go`](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tsp-go). This is Go's first transport binding, and the Go counterpart of the Rust `trust-tasks-tsp` crate and the Dart `trust_tasks_tsp` package (see #485).

## Why a separate module
The core `trust-tasks-go` module has **zero dependencies** — its selling point, and what the website claims. The TSP binding pulls in `affinidi-tsp-go` and its crypto (`circl`, `x/crypto`). A nested module keeps them apart: a consumer who only wants the types and the §7.2 pipeline still gets a dependency-free core. The core CI jobs run `./...` in `trust-tasks-go`, which **excludes** a nested module, so none of them pulls the TSP dependency; a dedicated `tsp` job builds and tests the binding on its own floor.

## API
- **`PackTrustTask(doc, sender, receiver)`** seals a **Direct** TSP message (HPKE authenticated encryption + signature). The payload is the envelope object `{"type": EnvelopeType, "document": <doc>}`.
- **`UnpackTrustTask(wire, recipient, sender)`** opens it, requires it to be sealed (signed-only is refused), checks the envelope type, and returns the document plus the authenticated sender. Failures come back as `*EnvelopeError` (`FailNotForThisReceiver`, `FailNotSealed`, `FailNotFinalRecipient`, `FailWrongEnvelopeType`, `FailInvalidBody`) — none answerable, since TSP has no anonymous sender (§4).
- **`Consumer` + `Receive[P, R]`** is the guarded inbound path: it runs `ConsumeInbound` with the item-11 duplicate-execution record and freshness bound **on by default**. Keyed on the document `id` (a re-forward is resealed with fresh material): a re-forward of the same document is absorbed with the first response; a different document under the same `id` is `idConflict`; a store that can't be consulted fails closed with `unavailable`; a handler error releases the claim. An in-band `issuer` that isn't the authenticated sender is `identityMismatch`, sealed back to the sender. Proofs are verified over the document as received.
- The Go TSP library does **no DID resolution** — the caller reads `AdvertisedSender(wire)` and supplies the sender `*tsp.Identity`, exactly as the Rust `unpack_trust_task` takes a resolved VID.

## Interop
The sealed `{type, document}` envelope matches the Rust crate and the Dart package byte-for-byte — a test opens a Go-sealed message and asserts the two-key object. Cross-implementation TSP wire interop rests on the shared TSP Rev 3 vectors the three TSP libraries each test against.

## Tests
39 subtests (`go test -race`): Direct round trip, the envelope-shape pin, confidentiality, wrong receiver, wrong sender, tamper, signed-only, foreign type, invalid body, no-encryption-key; and the consumer — identity omitted and TSP-supplied, reply round trip, re-forward absorbed, conflict, identity mismatch, recipient mismatch, staleness, proof without verifier, malformed payload, handler error releasing the claim, store failing closed, fire-and-forget. Plus a runnable godoc `Example`. gofmt- and vet-clean.

## Not released yet
`affinidi-tsp-go` has **no tag**, so `go.mod` requires it at a pseudo-version and there is **no `trust-tasks-go/tsp/v*` release wiring** in `publish.yml`. `go get github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go/tsp` already resolves the pseudo-version from the public repo, so the module is usable today. When `affinidi-tsp-go` is tagged: bump the requirement to the tag and add a `publish-go`-style tag job. RELEASING.md and CLAUDE.md record this.

## Follow-up
The website capability matrix still calls TSP Rust-only. Once the upstream TSP libraries (`affinidi-tsp-go`, `affinidi-tsp-dart`) are tagged/published, a follow-up should flip the Go and Dart TSP cells and update the now-outdated "TSP is dashed everywhere but Rust" note in `libraries.js`.

## Notes
The Go TSP library signs **Ed25519 only**, and `go 1.27` is inherited from `affinidi-tsp-go`.

title: feat(vta-service)!: tune the VTA's rate limits at runtime
body:
> **#1510 has merged; this PR was rebased onto `main`** — it now carries only the runtime-tuning half (2 commits) and full CI runs here.

## Diagnosis

After #1510 the VTA has separate `auth` and `did-log` limiters, but both were still `tower_governor` layers built once, with the router, from `[server]`. Nothing could change a quota without editing `config.toml` and restarting — exactly when an operator facing a wall of 429s can least afford a restart. The config registry (`operations::config::REGISTRY`, served by `config/patch/0.1` / `PATCH /config` / `pnm config update`) only knew `vta_did`, `vta_name` and `public_url`, and only string values.

## What changed

**Runtime-swappable limiter** (`vta-service/src/routes/rate_limit.rs`). The static `GovernorLayer` is replaced by our own axum middleware over `governor`'s keyed limiter. `governor` 0.10 was already in the lockfile via `tower_governor`; it is now a direct dependency of `vta-service` (no new crate in the graph — `Cargo.lock` only gains the edge). `tower_governor` stays for its client-IP key extractors, which are reused unchanged, so `trust_xff` attribution and its spoof-safety are identical.

- The running service (and the test harness) passes `QuotaSource::Live(state.config)`: each request reads the four `[server]` quotas from the shared config and, if a limiter's quota differs from the one its buckets were built for, swaps in fresh buckets. There is no push path to forget — any write to `config.server` (REST, Trust Task, DIDComm) takes effect on the next request.
- **A swap resets that limiter's buckets** (every IP starts from a full burst at the new quota). A patch that leaves a limiter's quota unchanged — an unrelated key, or the other limiter's quota — keeps its buckets. Documented in the module and the operator guide.
- `trust_xff` stays restart-only (it picks the extractor at router build).
- The 429 contract from #1510 is byte-identical: `x-rate-limit-source: vta`, `x-rate-limit-scope`, `retry-after` (now computed with a true ceiling rather than truncate + 1), `x-ratelimit-after`, JSON body. A request with no attributable client still gets the same 500 rather than passing unmetered.

**Registry keys** (`operations/config.rs`). `KeyDef` gains a value kind (`Text` / `Int { min, max }`). Four new keys — names taken from `vta_sdk::rate_limit` so the 429 hints and the registry cannot drift:

| key | kind | mutable | requires_restart |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rate_limit_interval_secs` | integer 1–3600 | yes | no |
| `rate_limit_burst` | integer 1–10000 | yes | no |
| `did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs` | integer 1–3600 | yes | no |
| `did_log_rate_limit_burst` | integer 1–10000 | yes | no |

Values are JSON integers (a string of decimal digits is also accepted); anything else, including `0`, is reported under `rejected` with the range. Persisted to `config.toml` like the existing keys and gated by the existing `require_super_admin`. `config/show` reports them as numbers with source `default` / `toml`.

**Audit.** A successful `config/patch` previously left no audit row on any transport: the dispatch spine records only *refusals* for non-vault tasks, leaving success to the handler, and this handler recorded nothing. Since loosening a rate limiter is a change to a security control, `update_config` now takes the audit sink and records one `config.update` row whose detail names each changed key and its new value (none are secret) — REST, Trust Task and DIDComm alike.

The config payload is not a new wire type: `config/patch/0.1`'s `overrides` is already `map<string, any JSON>` in the generated `trust_tasks_rs::specs::config::patch::v0_1::Payload`, so integers are representable without touching the spec or the SDK body type.

**CLI.** `pnm config update` and `cnm config update` gain `--rate-limit-interval-secs`, `--rate-limit-burst`, `--did-log-rate-limit-interval-secs`, `--did-log-rate-limit-burst` (sent as JSON integers). `config get` pads to the longest key so the new keys line up. In `vta-cli-common` this is additive: a new `cmd_config_patch` + `#[non_exhaustive] RateLimitOverrides`; `cmd_config_update` keeps its signature and delegates. A test in each CLI parses exactly the flags `vta_sdk::rate_limit::{VTA_RUNTIME_FLAGS, VTA_DID_LOG_RUNTIME_FLAGS}` print, so the #1511 hints fail a test rather than an operator if a flag is renamed.

**Docs.** New `docs/02-vta/rate-limiting.md` (the path `vta_sdk::rate_limit::VTA_DOCS` points at): what is and is not limited (JWT routes, DIDComm/TSP, `/health`), per-IP keying, `trust_xff` and the proxy trap, interval-vs-rate with worked examples, the TOML keys for `config.toml` / `vta setup --from`, runtime tuning and bounds, and how to tell a VTA 429 from the mediator's (`limits.rate_limit_per_ip` 100/s burst 50, optional per-DID), did-hosting-control's (30 / 60 s) and a proxy's. Linked from `docs/README.md`, `non-interactive-setup.md` and the setup example TOML. The CLAUDE.md "Rate limit" runtime guard now describes the split, the runtime keys and the header contract.

## Config / compatibility

- No config file changes needed; existing `[server]` keys keep their meaning.
- `vta-service`: `routes::router_with_cors(origins, trust_xff, RateLimits)` → `router_with_cors(origins, trust_xff, QuotaSource)` and `operations::config::update_config` gains an `audit_sink` parameter (hence the `!`); `routes::rate_limit` gains `QuotaSource`, `MAX_INTERVAL_SECS`, `MAX_BURST`.
- Final key names: `rate_limit_interval_secs`, `rate_limit_burst`, `did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs`, `did_log_rate_limit_burst` — identical to `vta_sdk::rate_limit`'s constants; flags identical to its `VTA_RUNTIME_FLAGS` / `VTA_DID_LOG_RUNTIME_FLAGS`; doc path identical to `VTA_DOCS`. `vta_sdk::rate_limit` needed no change.
- Known, pre-existing, unchanged: the keyed limiter's per-IP map is never pruned (as with `tower_governor` before); a swap does drop the old map.

## Tests

- `routes::rate_limit::tests` — a live quota change applies without rebuilding the router (loosen and tighten); an unrelated config change keeps bucket state; a live source honours the configured quota from the first request; no attributable client is refused, not unlimited; `ceil_secs`; plus #1510's independence, per-IP, 429-contract, SDK-label, zero-clamp and defaults tests on the new middleware.
- `operations::config::tests` — the four keys are mutable, live and integer; they are exactly the SDK's names; integer parsing bounds (0, max+1, negative, float, `"+5"`, `" 5"`, empty, bool, null all rejected); a patch updates memory and `config.toml` and `config/show` reports numbers; an out-of-range patch writes nothing; a non-super-admin is refused; defaults report `default`; an applied patch writes exactly one `config.update` audit row naming every key and value.
- `tests/api_integration.rs` — `PATCH /config` against the real router tightens the did-log burst to 2 and the next requests see it, loosens to 5 and they see that, and an out-of-range value changes nothing.
- `pnm-cli` / `cnm-cli` — `config update` parses the SDK hint's flags; `vta-cli-common` — overrides emit only set keys, as integers.
- The existing `rate_limit_tests` (governor interval-vs-rate semantics) are kept.

## Verification (local, this branch = #1510 rebased on `main` at #1511, plus this PR)

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | clean |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean (after fixing one `field_reassign_with_default` in a `vta-cli-common` test) |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm` | clean |
| `cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest,didcomm` | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` | 4430 passed, 0 failed (123 test binaries) |
| `cargo test -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm --lib routes::` | 59 passed |

`vtc-service` is untouched and its separate job was not run. `main` has since moved (#1512); this was not re-run on top of it.

title: fix(cli): type rate-limit refusals on the hand-rolled bootstrap and VTC paths
body:
## What

Three CLI paths build their own error strings from the HTTP status instead of going through the SDK client, so a **429 shows as a bare "request failed"** — the exact class #1511 fixed for the SDK paths:

- `pnm bootstrap connect` → `POST /bootstrap/request`
- `cnm` VTC backup export/import → VTC REST
- `cnm` audit verify → VTC REST

## Change

Each now maps a 429 to `VtaError::RateLimited` via `vta_sdk::error::VtaError::rate_limited_from_http` (response headers captured **before** the body consumes the response). `print_cli_error` already renders `RateLimited` with attribution (which service, the wait, how to tune it), so operators get the same guidance as every SDK path.

On `pnm bootstrap connect` the unauth limiter runs **before** the single-use carve-out is touched, so a 429 does not spend the enclave's one-shot first boot — the command prints a note that retrying after the wait is safe.

## Tests

The header parsing and source attribution live in `vta_sdk::rate_limit` / `VtaError::rate_limited_from_http`, which are unit-tested there. This PR is the call-site wiring; `cargo clippy -D warnings` and the workspace build cover it. Follows #1511 (merged).

## Notes

Completes the rate-limit-error work: #1511 typed the SDK paths; this closes the two hand-rolled CLI paths #1511's author explicitly left for a follow-up, plus `cnm audit verify` found by the same grep.

## [0.40.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.39.0...vta-sdk-v0.40.0) — 2026-09-16 ### Added - **tsp**: Adopt Rev 3, and give a TSP session a way to form a relationship ([#1512](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1512)) * docs(tsp): inventory what Rev 3 costs this repository Trust Spanning Protocol Rev 3 changed the crypto mode, the version byte, the long count-code prefix, the ciphertext code and layout, the `-E` count's meaning, the signature code and every payload layout at once. There is no compatibility mode: nothing a Rev 2 peer packs can be unpacked by a Rev 3 one, in either direction. So the stack flips together, and this repository is the last part of it with no plan written down. The inventory was produced by reading the `tsp-rev3` branch of affinidi-tdk-rs against this repository's own call sites, so it names files rather than describing intentions. Three things worth knowing without reading it: **The functional change is one arm.** §7.2.2 says an endpoint SHOULD drop an application message from a VID it holds no relationship with, and the SDK gates on that by default. SDK 0.22's `unpack_message` returns an `InboundTsp` enum instead of a payload, and its `Control` variant is what `handle_tsp` has to grow: record the invite, then decide whether to accept it. `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service`'s listener is a worked reference for the shape. **It fails silently.** A dropped message answers nothing, so a VTA that does not answer invites looks from every client like a transport that accepts connections and never replies. The wallet already sends the invite and waits five seconds before sending anyway, which means an unmigrated VTA that does not gate keeps working and one that does goes quiet — and neither state produces an error anyone can see. That is the reason this is written down before the work rather than during it. **There is an authorization decision to take.** Whether the VTA accepts an invite from any authenticated sender, or only from one the ACL already knows. The narrow reading breaks provisioning — a wallet talks to the VTA *in order to* be provisioned — so the broad one is almost certainly right, but it should be a decision rather than whatever the first implementer assumes. No code change. The work is blocked on an `affinidi-tdk` release carrying `affinidi-tsp` 0.2.0, and this workspace deliberately has no `[patch.crates-io]` to get ahead with — the note at the bottom of Cargo.toml records the duplicate-`vta-sdk` incident that removed it. - **sdk**: Type rate-limit refusals and say who sent them ([#1511](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1511)) A 429 became VtaError::Other("429: Too Many Requests"), with no hint and the Retry-After header discarded; through the boxed session auth path it became VtaError::Auth, telling the operator to re-authenticate. Add VtaError::RateLimited { limited_by, retry_after, limiter, url } with a non_exhaustive RateLimitSource (Vta, Vtc, Mediator, DidHost, Upstream) read from the x-rate-limit-source header; an unlabelled 429 is Upstream (proxy, load balancer, or older VTA). Every VTA HTTP status mapping in the SDK now reads headers. idempotent retries a rate limit whose wait fits MAX_RETRY_AFTER and surfaces a longer one at once. The CLI renders who refused, how long to wait, and which knob to turn; every key name lives in vta_sdk::rate_limit. ### Fixed - **backup**: Typed refusals for backup on a DIDComm/TSP-only VTA ([#1516](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1516)) The descriptor flow (`pnm backup export|import`) is REST-only: its `stream` algorithm moves the bytes over the VTA's HTTPS blob endpoint. A DIDComm/TSP-only VTA could not be backed up remotely, and every layer reported that badly. - SDK: `post_trust_task` refused DIDComm/TSP clients with `Validation` ("your request is wrong") although the same request succeeds over REST. It now returns `VtaError::UnsupportedTransport` naming `--transport rest`, as do `download_blob`/`upload_blob` when a client has no REST leg (their 429 → `RateLimited` mapping is unchanged). A DIDComm client's `rest_url` is still not used: it can come from the caller rather than from an advertised `VTARest` service, and the flow must not downgrade past what the peer advertises. - Server: a VTA with no `public_url` answered `initiate-*` with an opaque `internalError`, after already staging the bundle. It now refuses up front with the code `vta/backup/initiate-{export,import}/1.0` declare, `:transportUnavailable`, and the client maps that to `UnsupportedTransport`. - CLI: `--use-rest-legacy` on a DIDComm client silently sent the whole envelope as one mediator message (refused above 1 MiB, seen as a timeout). It now warns with the size caveat and `--transport rest`. Import no longer uploads the bytes twice: the commit finalizes the previewed bundle (new `VtaClient::backup_finalize_import`), and re-uploads only when the slot was already collected (not-found). A conflict is surfaced rather than retried, because it may mean "already committed" and commit is not idempotent. - retry_safety: initiate-export's reply carries the secret `transportToken`, not complete-export's; the classifications were swapped to match (initiate-export → KeyedSecret, complete-export → Keyed) so the token is never cached in the dedup store. - Docs: stale status line, non-existent offline `vta backup` command, the appstate note's claim that blobs work for DIDComm clients, the SDK "works on every transport" claim, and an operator note on backup for a DIDComm/TSP-only VTA. The planned transfer algorithm is renamed `chunkedTrustTask` (SPEC §4.10 casing) and specified upstream in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#474.

## `vta-config`
## [0.5.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-config-v0.4.9...vta-config-v0.5.0) — 2026-09-16 ### Added - **vta-service**: Give did.jsonl its own rate limiter and make VTA 429s attributable ([#1510](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1510)) * feat(vta-service)!: give did.jsonl its own rate limiter and make VTA 429s attributable One per-IP tower_governor bucket (burst 10, one token every 5 s) guarded the whole unauthenticated branch, including the public did.jsonl routes. A pnm command against a self-hosted VTA DID resolves the log and then runs challenge + authenticate from the same address, so a few commands in a row were refused; the mediator and the VTA's readiness gate fetch the log too. Serving the log is a store read with no crypto. - The DID-log routes (/.well-known/did.jsonl, the canonical catch-all, /did/{did}/log, TEE /attestation/did-log) move to their own per-IP limiter, keyed by trust_xff exactly as before, with new [server] keys did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs (default 1) and did_log_rate_limit_burst (default 60). The auth limiter keeps rate_limit_interval_secs / rate_limit_burst. The catch-all stays the only root wildcard, an opaque bare 404, rate-limited and body-capped. - Every 429 from a VTA limiter carries x-rate-limit-source: vta, x-rate-limit-scope (auth | did-log | backup-blob), a rounded-up Retry-After and a plain body naming the limiter, with no configuration values. - Public log responses send Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 and a strong sha256 ETag, and answer If-None-Match with 304. 404s carry neither. ### Fixed - **vta-service**: Trust a recent self-resolution instead of re-fetching per connect attempt ([#1509](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1509)) The mediator supervisor re-confirmed that the VTA's own DID resolves over the network before every connect attempt, and each confirmation built a throwaway DIDCacheClient and fetched did.jsonl uncached. For a VTA that hosts its own log, those fetches land on its own unauthenticated routes from its own address and share the per-IP rate limiter (10 burst, one token per 5 s by default) with everything else from that address. A run of connects failing for reasons that have nothing to do with resolvability (the mediator's negative cache, a mediator restart) spent that budget at one fetch per attempt, and the check straight after a passed gate fetched the document a second time. SelfResolutionProbe, owned by MessagingConnect and shared by the gate and every reconnect, remembers when a real network resolution last succeeded and answers from that for SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR (300 s). Each real check is still a fresh resolver built and stopped per check, so the preloaded self-DID entry cannot mask anything and no long-lived socket needs stopping on shutdown. Only successes are remembered: a failure clears the confirmation and the next attempt resolves again on the existing backoff. 300 s is the default mutable-method TTL of affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk, the resolver the mediator authenticates us through, so the mediator already acts on a copy of our document that old. If the document has become unresolvable inside the window, the connect's authcrypt check fails and the backoff governs the retry as before. run_gate and self_did_network_resolvable keep their signatures and behaviour; run_gate_with_probe and SelfResolutionProbe are additive.

title: feat(drivers): byte-exact deterministic packing for affinidi-rust and tsp-js
body:
Teaches the affinidi-rust and tsp-js drivers the protocol's `deterministic` capability, so their `pack-exact` vector cases run instead of skipping. Go and Dart already had it.

Each driver is gated on the library actually exposing the hook, so it still builds against a library that lacks it:
- **affinidi-rust:** `build.sh` enables the crate's `test-vectors` feature (and the driver's `deterministic`) only when the crate's manifest declares it. Against a crate without it, the build is unchanged and no capability is advertised. Lights up once affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#810 merges.
- **tsp-js:** the driver imports `dist/unsafe-testing.js` only if present (already shipped in vta-browser-plugin#252), the same feature-detection it uses for `resolveAccept`.

Both route `pack` with `ephemeral` (`ikmE`/`skEm`) to the library's deterministic packer and map `payloadSender: null` and `pad` nonces where the vectors need them; unsupported combinations still answer `unsupported`.

**Verified** against the fixed libraries (seed 20260916, `--gate known`, 0 unexplained): pack-exact passes for all 9 classical vectors on affinidi-rust, Go and Dart; the 6 HPKE-Base vectors on tsp-js; and signed-only on the reference. Vectors suite rose from 137 to 152 passing.

The committed `reports/report.md` will refresh on the next CI run once #810 is merged and the affinidi-rust capability is live on `main`.

body:
Release PR for the Dart package `trust_tasks_proof`, the counterpart to the release-plz PR for the
crates and the `release-ts` / `release-go` PRs. **Merging this starts the
release**: the `tag-dart` job in `publish.yml` verifies the package and pushes
`trust-tasks-dart-proof-v0.1.1`, and that tag triggers `publish-dart.yml`, which
publishes to pub.dev over OIDC.

- `trust_tasks_proof`: `0.1.0` → `0.1.1` (`patch`)
- derived from the conventional commits in `trust-tasks-dart-proof-v0.1.0..HEAD` touching `trust-tasks-dart-proof`

Unlike the other three, pub.dev refuses a publish that was not triggered by a tag
push — so the tag is a step in the chain rather than a record of one. If
`RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` is unset the tag is pushed by the default token, which does
not trigger workflows; `tag-dart` warns when that happens and the fix is to
re-push the tag from a workstation.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(tsp-js): merged-spec (AAC) vectors, re-packed byte for byte
body:
This PR targets `feat/tsp-rev2-rev3-dual-handler`, like #249, #250 and #251.

**1. Vectors move to the merged spec.** `tests/fixtures/spec-rev3-vectors.json` held the pre-merge `YTSP-ABA` vectors. It now holds the Appendix A vectors from trustoverip/tswg-tsp-specification@f5b8668 (`YTSP-AAC`), which changed every message and the control-message digests.
- Tests that hard-coded ABA are updated.
- A new test pins one old ABA message, so reading Rev 3 at MINOR 64 stays covered.
- Library behaviour is unchanged.

**2. Byte-exact re-pack.** tsp-js could open the vectors but not reproduce them, so an encoder bug that two implementations share went undetected. A new subpath, `@openvtc/vti-tsp-js/unsafe-testing`, exports `__unsafeDeterministic*` packers.
- They derive the HPKE ephemeral from the vector's published `ikmE` (RFC 9180 DeriveKeyPair).
- They can write the NULL ESSR sender, which every published vector uses.
- The root entry point is unchanged and exposes none of this. The module header explains why a fixed ephemeral breaks confidentiality and integrity.

**Reviewer decision:** the subpath is listed in `package.json` `exports`, so it ships in the published package, clearly named. If you'd rather it not ship at all, the alternative is a test-only import from `dist/`.

**Results:**
- All six HPKE-Base vectors now re-pack byte for byte: `direct-hpke-base`, `control-rfi-direct`, `control-rfa-direct`, `control-rfd`, `nested-direct`, `routed`.
- `direct-sealed-box`, `control-rfi-sealed-box` and `direct-signed-only` aren't covered, because tsp-js has no packer for those schemes.
- `direct-hpke-base-pq` publishes no ephemeral material.

**Tests:**
- tsp-js `npm test`: 124 pass.
- core `tests/tsp.*.mjs`: 33 pass.
- With the matching conformance-driver change, the suite's `pack-exact` cases pass for tsp-js on the same six vectors.

title: fix(vta-sdk): resolve each DID once per process through a shared resolver
body:
## Root cause

A VTA that self-hosts its `did:webvh` log could trip its own per-IP unauthenticated rate limiter (default burst 10, one token per 5 s, shared with `/auth/*`). On the client side, the SDK spent that budget before it had authenticated.

Every SDK path that resolves a DID without being handed a resolver built a throwaway resolver per call:

- `session::resolve_vta_endpoint`, `rest_url_from_did_doc` (behind `resolve_vta_url`) and `resolve_mediator_did` each built a new `DIDCacheClient`.
- `VtaClient::resolve_did` built one per call.
- `display_name::agent_name::fill_book` built one per call.
- Each `VtaClient` built its own reply-proof-verification resolver.
- `didcomm_light::resolve_webvh_keyagreement` called `didwebvh-rs`'s `DIDWebVHState::resolve` directly, with no cache at all.

A fresh client has an empty cache. One CLI command therefore fetched the VTA's `did.jsonl` several times over (transport discovery, mediator lookup, REST URL, reply verification), each fetch coming from the same address as the authentication calls that followed.

## Change

`vta_sdk::resolver::shared_did_resolver(url)` (plus `shared_did_resolver_from_env()` and `shutdown_shared_did_resolvers()`) returns one `DIDCacheClient` per (tokio runtime, resolver URL, host policy). It is built on first use with the existing `build_did_cache_config`, so the TDK cache answers every repeat. That cache holds `did:web`/`did:webvh` results for 300 s, caches only successes, and single-flights concurrent misses. A failure is always fetched again.

Every site above now uses it. So does `pnm health`'s own resolver, so its checks and the SDK calls it makes share one cache.

- **Why the runtime is in the key.** A `DIDCacheClient` is not runtime-neutral: a network-mode client's websocket task and pooled connections belong to the runtime that built it. A sentinel task spawned on that runtime marks the entry dead when the runtime shuts down. On the next lookup, dead entries are `stop()`ped and dropped. `shutdown_shared_did_resolvers()` stops them all, for an embedder that wants the sidecar socket closed before its runtime ends. A client that loses a construction race is stopped immediately.
- **No auto-trait change.** The map is a `static`, and `VtaClient` and every other public struct are untouched. The `tokio::sync::OnceCell` auto-trait trap does not apply.
- **Trust boundaries kept.**
  - Reply verification honours `PNM_RESOLVER_URL` (`shared_did_resolver_from_env()`), like the session entry points. Resolving it locally defeated a configured cache and let the signer's host rate-limit verification. This folds in #1515, which is closed in favour of this PR.
  - `didcomm_light` resolves in **local** mode (`shared_did_resolver(None)`), as before.
  - Host policy is re-read per call, and a change to it gets its own client, so a cache filled under `AllowPrivate` is never served under `PublicOnly`.
- **Dependency changes.**
  - `didwebvh-rs` is no longer a dependency of the `client` feature; the cache SDK's `did:webvh` resolver runs the same log verification. It stays as a dev-dependency so the new test can mint a real log.
  - `proof-verify` and `agent-names` now enable `dep:tokio`.
  - The workspace `tokio` requirement goes from `1` to `1.49`, where `runtime::Id` was stabilised. The lockfile already resolves 1.53.

## Behaviour change to note

Within one process, repeat resolutions of the same DID now return the cached document for up to 300 s. For the CLIs that is the point. A long-lived embedder calling these entry points sees the same TTL every other `DIDCacheClient` in the stack already applies. For example, `vta-mcp`'s `resolve_did` now serves a document changed by `services … enable` up to 5 minutes stale.

## Compatibility

Additive public API only: three new functions in `resolver`. No signature, struct or enum changes, so no `!`. I did not run `cargo semver-checks` locally.

## Tests

`vta-sdk/tests/shared_did_resolver.rs` is its own binary, because it allows loopback hosts process-wide. It serves a **real signed `did:webvh` log** from a local wiremock server and counts `GET /.well-known/did.jsonl` requests:

- `every_entry_point_shares_one_fetch_of_the_same_did`: two rounds of `resolve_vta_endpoint`, `resolve_mediator_did`, `resolve_vta_url` and `didcomm_light::resolve_vta_keyagreement` cost **1** fetch in total. The test also asserts the served document was used, not the URL fallback.
- `a_failed_resolution_is_fetched_again`: two 404s are fetched twice, the first success is fetched, and the repeats are not.
- `a_later_runtime_gets_a_working_resolver`: sequential runtimes each get a working client rather than a dead one.

## Verification (local, macOS, after rebasing onto #1511)

Run on a tree with this commit plus the independent readiness PR #1509:
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- both reduced-feature `vta-service` clippy runs from `ci.yml`: clean
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast`: 4406 passed, 0 failed, 50 ignored. The 3 new tests ran.
- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast`: 1644 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored
- `cargo check -p vta-sdk` under `--all-features --all-targets`, and under `--no-default-features` with each of `proof-verify`, `agent-names` and `client`: builds

title: ci(release): give the Release PR job the time its semver check now needs
body:
**#1506 is stale and nothing says so.** `Release-plz PR` was cancelled at its
30-minute timeout when #1512 merged, so the Release PR still describes a `main`
from before Rev 3 landed — it would publish `vta-sdk 0.40.0` built against
`affinidi-tdk 0.14`, which is exactly the build that does *not* clear the
`vta-sdk` dependency cycle.

## Why it timed out

The job's cost scales with **how many crates changed since their last release**
— release-plz semver-checks each one against its published baseline. An
ordinary merge touches a few; #1512 moved every `affinidi-*` pin at once.

Same workflow, same day:

| Run | Duration | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 07:09 | 19m 14s | success |
| 09:32 | 20m 11s | success |
| 12:59 | 22m 58s | success |
| **15:08** (merge of #1512) | **30m 26s** | **cancelled** |

The budget had been creeping toward the ceiling for a while and that merge went
through it. For scale, CI's own `semver report` job covers a broader crate set,
is given **45** minutes, and uses 41–44 of them. 60 matches
`release-plz-release` and leaves headroom rather than the thin margin that just
failed.

## The part worth reading

This failure is silent in the way that matters. The job is **cancelled** rather
than failed, `Release-plz release` beside it stays green, and the Release PR is
left describing an older `main` — no error on the PR, nothing red pointing at
it, and it still looks mergeable. Merging it would publish a coherent-looking
release built against the wrong dependency set.

That is the same stale-Release-PR hazard the concurrency note in this file
already documents, reached by a different route. The comment now says what to do
about it: **read a Release PR's `updatedAt` against main's HEAD before merging
it; do not assume it regenerated.**

Not a new timeout policy — the swapfile step above trades memory pressure for
wall-clock, so this job was always going to be slower than its raw work
suggests.

## Effect

Merging this re-triggers the regeneration, so #1506 comes back in line with
post-Rev-3 `main` as a side effect of the fix.

title: feat(dart-didcomm): DIDComm v2.1 transport binding for Dart (trust_tasks_didcomm)
body:
Adds **`trust_tasks_didcomm`**, the DIDComm v2.1 transport binding (`bindings/didcomm/0.2`) for Dart. It is built on Affinidi's `package:didcomm` and is the Dart counterpart of the Rust `trust-tasks-didcomm` crate. This is the third and last of the agreed Dart packages.

## Envelope layer
- **`packTrustTask`** always uses authcrypt (ECDH-1PU). It sets `thid` and `pthid` from the document's `threadId` and `parentThreadId`, falling back to the document `id` (§3.1).
- **`unpackTrustTask`** returns the document exactly as the sender serialised it, plus the authenticated sender and the recipient.
  - The sender is taken from the `skid` of the ECDH-1PU layer. It is never guessed, and a `skid` without a key fragment is an error.
  - The wrapping is judged from the layers didcomm reports, not from its error text. Anoncrypt, signed-only and plaintext messages are refused.
  - `allowedSenders` is checked **before decryption**, because opening an envelope resolves the sender's DID, and a `did:web` means fetching from a host the sender chose.
  - A DIDComm message of any other type is refused.
- Envelope-layer failures throw a typed `EnvelopeException`. No reply is possible for these (§4), because there is no authenticated sender to address it to.

## Consumer: `DidcommConsumer`
- Unpacks the envelope, checks the thread headers, then runs `consumeInbound` with the duplicate-execution record and freshness bound **on by default**.
- The record is keyed on the document `id`, never the DIDComm `id` or `thid`. A mediator redelivery arrives as a fresh DIDComm message around the same document, and is absorbed as a duplicate that gets the first response back.
- A different document under the same `id` gets `idConflict`. If the record can't be consulted, the consumer answers `unavailable` without executing.
- If the handler throws, the claim is released, so a redelivery runs again.
- If a body from an authenticated sender doesn't deserialise, the consumer answers with `malformedRequest` rather than throwing (§4), because it knows who to reply to.
- A `thid` that disagrees with `threadId` gets `malformedRequest`, not `identityMismatch` (§3.1).
- An in-band `issuer` that isn't the authenticated sender gets `identityMismatch`, addressed to the sender that actually authenticated.
- Proofs are verified over the document as it arrived. With no verifier configured, a proof-bearing document is refused rather than having its proof ignored.
- `received.reply` holds the document to send back, and `packReply` authcrypts it to the authenticated sender.

## Interop (run, not assumed)
Uses fixed did:key identities, with the Rust side's X25519 key checked against the Dart DID document's `keyAgreement`:

| Direction | Result |
|---|---|
| Dart packs → Rust `unpack_trust_task` → Rust replies → Dart unpacks | ✓ Rust authenticates the Dart sender; the reply opens in Dart with `thid` and `threadId` intact |
| Rust packs → Dart `DidcommConsumer` (then a redelivery) → Dart replies → Rust unpacks | ✓ handled, then `DuplicateOutcome`; the reply opens in Rust |

## Tests
25 in total:
- Round trips with P-256 and Ed25519 keys.
- Thread headers, and a distinct DIDComm `id` per pack.
- Refusals: wrong recipient, tampered ciphertext, anoncrypt, plaintext, signed-only, allowlist, foreign type, invalid body.
- The consumer: identity omitted and supplied by authcrypt, the reply round trip, redelivery, conflict, identity mismatch, recipient mismatch, thread mismatch, staleness, proof without a verifier, malformed proof and payload, a handler exception, the store failing closed, and fire-and-forget.

## pana
150/160 on this branch. The only miss is the repository-URL check, which can't pass until the package is on `main`. `package:didcomm` pins ssi 3, so `pqcrypto` isn't in the graph and documentation scores full marks. Web isn't supported, because `package:didcomm` itself isn't; the platform check still gives full points.

## Also in this PR
- Plumbing: CI jobs for SDK 3.6 and stable, the tag and Release PR matrices, the publish tag pattern, and the release script case.
- The website's Dart DIDComm v2 cell changes from ◐ to ●.
- The Dart HTTPS and DIDComm packages are now listed on their binding pages (`bindings.js`). #481 missed the HTTPS one.
- Stale site copy corrected: the Rust card said it was "the only one with transports today", and the ecosystem entry said transports ship only in Rust.

## After merge (maintainer)
1. Run `dart pub publish` from `trust-tasks-dart-didcomm/`.
2. Enable trusted publishing with tag pattern `trust-tasks-dart-didcomm-v{{version}}`.

title: fix(backup): typed refusals for backup on a DIDComm/TSP-only VTA
body:
Backup and restore (`pnm backup export|import`) use the descriptor pattern. Its only transfer algorithm, `stream`, moves the bytes over the VTA's HTTPS blob endpoint, so a VTA that speaks only DIDComm or TSP cannot be backed up remotely. Every layer reported that badly. This PR makes each refusal typed and accurate, and fixes the docs that said otherwise.

## SDK
- `post_trust_task` refused DIDComm/TSP clients with `VtaError::Validation`, which reads as "your request is wrong" even though the same request succeeds over REST. It now returns `VtaError::UnsupportedTransport`, whose doc describes this exact case, and the message names `--transport rest`. `download_blob`/`upload_blob` do the same when a client has no REST leg. Their 429 → `RateLimited` handling from #1511 is kept.
- A DIDComm/TSP client's optional `rest_url` still does not open the flow. It can come from the caller rather than from a `VTARest` service in the VTA's DID document, and CLAUDE.md forbids downgrading past what the peer advertises.
- The client maps a `…:transportUnavailable` Trust Task error to `UnsupportedTransport`.
- New `VtaClient::backup_finalize_import` (additive).

## Server
- A VTA with no `public_url` answered `initiate-export`/`initiate-import` with an opaque `internalError`, and only after it had already staged the bundle. It now refuses with the code the published specs declare, `vta/backup/initiate-{export,import}:transportUnavailable`.
  - The check runs after the super-admin gate and before anything is staged, so no orphan bundle is left behind.
  - The wire message names no config key; the log does.

## CLI (`pnm backup`)
- `--use-rest-legacy` on a DIDComm client did not use REST. It sent the whole envelope as one mediator message, which a mediator refuses above 1 MiB and which surfaces as a timeout. It now warns with that size caveat and points at `--transport rest`. The flag is kept for compatibility.
- Import no longer uploads the bytes twice. The commit finalizes the bundle the preview already uploaded.
  - It re-uploads only if the slot has been collected, which shows up as not-found.
  - A conflict is surfaced with guidance instead of being retried. It can mean "already committed", and commit is not idempotent.

## retry_safety
The comment said `complete-export` returns the encrypted state. In fact `initiate-export`'s reply carries the secret `transportToken`, and `complete-export` returns only `{bundleId, downloaded}`. The two classifications were swapped to match: `initiate-export` is now `KeyedSecret` and `complete-export` is `Keyed`, so the token never sits in the dedup store.

## Docs
- `backup-descriptor-pattern.md`: fixed the stale "Status: spec only" line. The future-work text now describes the specified `chunkedTrustTask` algorithm, renamed from `chunked-trust-task` per trusttasks SPEC §4.10 casing.
- `trust-task-uri-registry.md`: same update.
- `appstate-store.md` §5: corrected the claim that blobs work for DIDComm clients that have a REST URL. `post_trust_task`'s gate refuses them first.
- `non-interactive-setup.md`, `seal-and-unseal.md`, `backup-descriptor-pattern.md`: removed references to an offline `vta backup` command that never existed, and replaced them with the real procedure (`pnm backup export|import` against a running VTA).
- `vta-sdk/src/client/backup.rs`: corrected the "works on every transport" claim.
- New operator note "Backup on a DIDComm/TSP-only VTA" in `docs/02-vta/runtime-service-management.md`: today's limitation, what to do before disabling REST, and the planned chunked path.

Upstream spec for that path: trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#474 (merged; released in `trust-tasks-rs` 0.21.1).

## Tests
- The transport gate lets REST through and refuses DIDComm/TSP with `UnsupportedTransport`, naming the fix and the surface. A REST client is not refused by the gate.
- `…:transportUnavailable` maps to `UnsupportedTransport` on the client.
- The server's `transportUnavailable` rejection carries `<slug>:transportUnavailable` for both initiate tasks, is not a 500, and does not leak `public_url`.
- `blob_transport_base_url` treats an unset or blank `public_url` as unavailable.
- The `--use-rest-legacy` warning fires on DIDComm/TSP and not on REST.

## Verification (after rebasing onto #1511)
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: exit 0
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast`: exit 0, 4406 passed, 0 failed, 50 ignored
- `vtc-service`/`vtc-client` were not run: nothing here touches them beyond additive `vta-sdk` API.

## Not in this PR: waits on the spec, now released
- The `chunkedTrustTask` implementation:
  - server handlers for `initiate-{export,import}/1.1`, `get-chunk/1.0`, `put-chunk/1.0` and `finalize-import/1.1`
  - chunk staging and serving
  - a TTL extended by activity, up to a ceiling
  - a per-DID chunk rate limit
  - an SDK client that pulls, verifies and resumes chunks
  - lifting the DIDComm/TSP refusal in this PR
- The `trust-tasks-rs` 0.21 bump. It carries TSP Rev 3 and is in #1512.
- The follow-up implementation PR will be stacked on this one.

title: fix(vtc): say which limiter refused on every VTC 429
body:
An operator refused with a bare 429 could not tell whether the VTC, a VTA, a
mediator, a DID host or a proxy in front of any of them had done it. Every 429
the VTC's own limiters emit now carries the ecosystem attribution contract:
`x-rate-limit-source: vtc`, `Retry-After: <seconds>` (never 0), and an
`application/json` body
`{"error":"rate_limited","limiter":"<name>","message":"...","retryAfterSecs":N}`.
The header name comes from `vta_sdk::rate_limit::SOURCE_HEADER` (#1511), and
tests read each refusal back through `VtaError::rate_limited_from_http` as
`RateLimitSource::Vtc`, so server and client cannot drift.

Limiters covered:

- `unauth`: the per-IP tower-governor on the unauthenticated chain (auth,
  wallet auth, passkey login, install claim start/finish, recognise,
  relationships publish, POST /v1/trust-tasks). Reshaped with a governor
  error handler; key-extraction failures keep their 500.
- `relationships`: the per-member publish window. It used to refuse with a
  400 `AppError::Validation`; it now returns a 429 whose Retry-After is when
  the oldest counted publication leaves the window.

There are no other request limiters in vtc-service; the install claim secret
relies on the unauth governor. Neither limiter is on the DIDComm/TSP dispatch
path, and the Trust Task framework defines no rate-limit error code, so no
Trust Task error document reports one.

Also corrects prose calling the governor "5 rps": `per_second(5)` is a
replenishment interval (a burst of 10, then one request per 5 s).

The publish route documents the 429 with a `RateLimitedBody` schema, so the
OpenAPI snapshot and the generated admin-ui wire types are regenerated.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast`: all 63 test targets pass, including the new `tests/rate_limit_source.rs`, `pairwise::a_member_over_the_publish_allowance_gets_the_rate_limit_contract`, and the regenerated `openapi_snapshot`

title: feat(cli): name removal commands `delete`, and say what a delete leaves behind
body:
Removal commands across `pnm`, `cnm` and the offline `vta` CLI are now named `delete`. Every old name still parses, as a hidden alias, so no script breaks. That's why the title has no `!`: the syntax the CLIs accept only grows, and no published crate's public API changes. `vta-cli-common` keeps `cmd_webvh_server_remove` / `cmd_memory_forget` under their existing names for that reason. Trust Task URIs are unchanged (`spec/vta/webvh/servers/remove/1.0` is a specification name).

Where a `delete` doesn't delete everything, the command now prints a notice saying what remains and the command that removes it.

## Renamed

| Old | New | Old name kept as | Notice added |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pnm did-mgmt servers remove <id>` | `pnm did-mgmt servers delete <id>` | hidden alias `remove` | Lists DIDs still registered against the server, notes their logs are still hosted there, and prints the `servers add --id … --did …` + `dids delete` sequence that removes them completely. The lookup is best-effort, and the delete never refuses. |
| `vta did-mgmt servers remove <id>` (offline) | `vta did-mgmt servers delete <id>` | hidden alias `remove` | same, read from the local store |
| `pnm vta remove <slug>` | `pnm vta delete <slug>` | hidden alias `remove` | Only the local connection and credential are deleted. The VTA's ACL entry remains, and the notice prints `pnm acl delete <client-did>`, with a warning not to run it for the VTA's only admin |
| `cnm community remove <name>` | `cnm community delete <name>` (+ `--yes/-y`, hidden `--force`) | hidden alias `remove` | same, with `cnm acl delete <client-did>` |
| `pnm memory forget <key>` | `pnm memory delete <key>` | hidden alias `forget` (`delete` used to be the hidden alias) | — |
| `vta approvals disable` | `vta approvals delete-all` | hidden subcommand `disable`, which prints a note naming `delete-all` and then runs it | — |
| internal `WebvhCommands::RemoveServer` (pnm + vta) | `DeleteServer` | n/a (not user-facing) | — |

`pnm vault delete` / `pnm cred-vault delete` without `--force` now also print how to delete right away: `vault purge <id>` (or `vault delete <id> --force`). `vault purge` / `cred-vault purge` stay visible. Their help text now says they do the same thing as `delete --force`, which the server handler confirms: `force: true` and `purge` both call the same hard delete.

### Judgement calls
- **`vta vault wipe` keeps its name.** It is a bulk hard delete, like `pnm memory wipe`, and cli-style.md now allows a bulk verb as long as the help text says it deletes every entry. Its confirmation flag becomes `--yes` (hidden `--force`), because it was a consent flag, not a "skip the soft delete" flag.
- **`vta approvals delete-all`, not `delete --all`.** There is no `delete <one>` to pair with `--all`: deleting a single rule is `remove`, which keeps its verb (below).
- **No refusal on `servers delete` with DIDs still registered.** A refusal would change what the Trust Task does, and would break any script that deletes such a server today. It prints the notice instead. See the follow-up below: that notice matters more than it first appears.

## Kept the verb (not deletion)

| Command | Why |
|---|---|
| `pnm approvals remove`, `approvals approvers remove` (and offline `vta approvals remove`) | Edits a list inside one policy row; the row survives |
| `pnm did-mgmt agent-names remove` | Releases a name claim, next to `enable`/`disable`. Help now says the released name can be claimed by any DID, and points to `disable` to park it |
| `pnm keys revoke` / `cnm keys revoke` | Changes a key's lifecycle state |
| `cnm vetting vetters revoke` | Credential revocation |
| `pnm device disable` / `device wipe` | The device stays on record; `wipe` is a remote-wipe instruction, not record deletion |
| `services * disable` | Withdraws an advertisement, and `rollback` can restore it |
| `services didcomm drain cancel` | Stops a pending process |
| `auth logout` | Ends a session |

## `--force` / `--yes` rule (written up in `docs/04-reference/cli-style.md`)

- `--yes` / `-y` skips a confirmation prompt, or is the consent a non-interactive run gives. It never changes what gets deleted.
- On a delete, `--force` means skip the soft delete, and only where a soft path exists (`vault delete`, `cred-vault delete`).
- Prompt-skipping commands that used to take `--force` / `-f` still accept them as hidden aliases of `--yes`:
  - `pnm contexts delete`, `cnm contexts delete`, `vta contexts delete` (`--force`, `-f`)
  - `pnm vta delete` (`--force`)
  - `vta did-mgmt dids delete` (`--force`)
  - `vta vault wipe` (`--force`)
  - `pnm memory wipe` (already did; now also takes `-y`)
- The other uses of `--force` are not about deletion and are unchanged: `backup export --force` (overwrite the output file), `did-mgmt dids register --force` (take over a slot), `services didcomm {enable,update} --force` (skip the handshake), `vta vault seed --force` (overwrite an entry).

## Knock-on
- Hints in `pnm-cli/src/setup.rs` now name `pnm vta delete`. One of them also pointed at `pnm vta show {slug}`, which doesn't exist; it now says `pnm --vta {slug} vta info`.
- Docs updated: `docs/02-vta/{approvals,non-interactive-setup,personal-ai-agents}.md`, `docs/05-design-notes/{pnm-setup-deferred-vta-did,approvals-convergence}.md`, `pnm-cli/README.md`, `cnm-cli/README.md`.
- Parse tests cover every new name, every kept alias, and each `--yes`/`--force`/`-f` spelling (pnm, cnm, vta). `vta-service/tests/approvals_breakglass_cli.rs` now drives `delete-all`, and has a new test showing `disable` still deletes everything and names `delete-all`.

## Follow-up found, not fixed here
`dids delete` on a DID whose server id is no longer registered removes the local record and **skips the delete on the hosting server without reporting it**. In `operations::did_webvh` `delete_did`, `get_server` returning `None` sets no `daemon_cleanup_error`, so the log is left orphaned on the host and nothing is reported. The `servers delete` notice tells operators to re-add the server before deleting such DIDs. The operation itself should probably report the skip, but that is a server-side behaviour change and out of scope for a naming PR.

The root `CLAUDE.md` still says `vta approvals {list,remove,disable}` in the approvals section. I left it for a maintainer to update.

## Verification
All run on the branch after rebasing onto `origin/main` at e7c70ef3 (#1511):
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast`: exit 0, 123 test binaries and doc-test runs, 4406 tests passed, 0 failed. All the new parse tests and approvals break-glass tests ran and passed.
- `vtc-service` / `vtc-client` were not run; this PR changes neither.

title: feat(vta-service)!: give did.jsonl its own rate limiter and make VTA 429s attributable
body:
## Diagnosis

`routes::apply_unauth_governor` put **one** per-IP `tower_governor` bucket (default burst 10, one token every 5 s) in front of the whole unauthenticated branch — the auth endpoints *and* the public `did.jsonl` routes (`/.well-known/did.jsonl`, the `/{*did_log_path}` catch-all, `/did/{did}/log`, TEE `/attestation/did-log`).

For a VTA that hosts its own `did:webvh` log, every `pnm` command resolves the VTA DID (an uncached `did.jsonl` GET) and then runs challenge + authenticate from the same address — 3 of the 10 tokens — so a few commands in a row got 429. The mediator and the VTA's own readiness gate fetch the log too. Serving the log is a store read with no crypto; it was spending a budget sized for endpoints that do crypto on caller input. The 429 itself was tower_governor's bare `Too Many Requests! Wait for Ns`, which gave an operator no way to tell the VTA's limiter from a mediator's or a proxy's.

## What changed

**Separate limiters** (`vta-service/src/routes/rate_limit.rs`, new). Each branch gets its own per-IP buckets, still keyed by `trust_xff` exactly as before (`PeerIpKeyExtractor` / `SmartIpKeyExtractor`):

| scope | routes | quota |
|---|---|---|
| `auth` | auth challenge/authenticate/refresh, passkey login, `/bootstrap/request`, TEE attestation reports | `rate_limit_interval_secs` / `rate_limit_burst` (5 / 10, unchanged) |
| `did-log` | `/.well-known/did.jsonl`, the canonical catch-all, `/did/{did}/log`, TEE `/attestation/did-log` | **new** `did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs` / `did_log_rate_limit_burst` (1 / 60) |
| `backup-blob` | `/backup/blob/*` | auth quota, own bucket (as before) |

The catch-all stays the only root wildcard, still answers an opaque bare 404, and is still rate-limited (now on `did-log`) and body-capped at `UNAUTH_BODY_SIZE`. `/attestation/did-log` moved with the other log routes — same public log, same cheap read.

**Attributable 429s.** Every 429 any VTA limiter produces now carries:

- `x-rate-limit-source: vta` — **a client contract; do not rename.**
- `x-rate-limit-scope: auth | did-log | backup-blob`
- `retry-after: <secs>` (rounded *up*, never 0 — tower_governor truncates, so a client honouring it was being refused again) and the legacy `x-ratelimit-after` with the same value
- `application/json` body — no configuration values:

```json
{"error":"rate_limited","limiter":"did-log","message":"Too Many Requests: rejected by the VTA's `did-log` rate limiter. Retry after 3 s.","retryAfterSecs":3}
```

This is the server half of the contract #1511 (`vta_sdk::rate_limit`, merged) reads: the header name and the legacy wait header come from `vta_sdk::rate_limit::{SOURCE_HEADER, LEGACY_RETRY_AFTER_HEADER}` rather than literals, and a test asserts `RateLimitSource::from_source_header(Some("vta"))` is `Vta`, so server and client cannot drift. The config key names this PR adds are the ones `vta_sdk::rate_limit::{VTA_DID_LOG_INTERVAL_KEY, VTA_DID_LOG_BURST_KEY}` already name. Implemented through `GovernorLayer::error_handler`; the key-extraction 500 is unchanged.

**Cacheable logs.** The public log responses now send `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` and a strong `ETag` (`"sha256-<hex>"` over the log bytes), and answer a matching `If-None-Match` (exact, list, weak form or `*`) with `304` and no body. 60 s is well inside the 300 s that `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` (the resolver the mediator and clients use) already caches a `did:webvh` document for, so an HTTP cache adds no staleness a verifier does not already accept; the log is append-only, so a cached copy is at worst missing the newest entry. Caching headers are only ever set on 200/304 — a 404 stays byte-identical to axum's default, so they cannot fingerprint the DID configuration.

## Config / compatibility

- `vta-config::ServerConfig` gains `did_log_rate_limit_interval_secs` and `did_log_rate_limit_burst` (serde defaults, so existing `config.toml` files load unchanged). `ServerConfig` is not `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a struct literal elsewhere breaks — hence the `!`.
- `vta-service`: `routes::router_with_cors(origins, trust_xff, interval_secs, burst)` → `router_with_cors(origins, trust_xff, RateLimits)`; the `pub(crate)` `UNAUTH_INTERVAL_SECS` / `UNAUTH_BURST` consts moved into `routes::rate_limit`. New public `routes::rate_limit` module (`Limiter`, `Quota`, `RateLimits`, header-name consts).
- `vta setup` (interactive) writes the new defaults; `vta setup --from` already takes `[server]` as a `ServerConfig`, so the keys flow through.
- Zero in either new key clamps to 1, like the existing keys.
- Operationally: the auth budget is unchanged; `did.jsonl` fetches simply stop spending it.

Runtime tuning of all four keys and operator docs follow in a stacked PR.

## Tests

- `routes::rate_limit::tests` — a did-log burst does not spend the auth budget and vice versa (two limiters merged into one router, same shape as `build_api_router`); per-IP isolation; the full 429 contract (headers, `retry-after ≥ 1`, exact JSON body); the source label is what the SDK reads as `Vta`; zero clamp for all four keys; defaults match `ServerConfig::default()`.
- `tests/api_integration.rs` — end-to-end on the real router: a `did.jsonl` flood (both the well-known route and the catch-all) trips `did-log` no earlier than its 60 burst and leaves the same IP's full auth burst; an auth flood leaves `did.jsonl` reachable; the existing auth and backup-blob 429 tests now also assert `x-rate-limit-source` / `x-rate-limit-scope`.
- `routes::self_hosted_did::tests` — strong ETag + `max-age=60` on 200; 304 with no body for exact / listed / weak / `*`; a stale tag gets the full log; the tag changes when the log grows; 404s carry no caching headers even with `If-None-Match: *`.
- `vta-config` — the new keys default, parse, and are not flagged as unknown.
- The existing `rate_limit_tests` (tower_governor interval-vs-rate semantics) and `zero_rate_limit_config_is_clamped_not_panicked` are kept.

## Verification (local, on this branch, rebased on `main` at #1511)

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | clean |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm` | clean |
| `cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest,didcomm` | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` | 4414 passed, 0 failed (123 test binaries) |
| `cargo test -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm --lib routes::` | 53 passed (before the rebase onto #1511; the TEE path is unchanged by it) |

`vtc-service` is untouched and its separate job was not run.

title: fix(vta-service): trust a recent self-resolution instead of re-fetching per connect attempt
body:
## Root cause

A VTA that self-hosts its `did:webvh` log could trip its own per-IP unauthenticated rate limiter (default burst 10, one token per 5 s, shared with `/auth/*`).

Part of the resolution volume came from the mediator supervisor. `MessagingConnect::supervise` called `readiness::self_did_network_resolvable` before **every** connect attempt. `self_did_resolves` deliberately builds a throwaway `DIDCacheClient` per call, so that the startup-preloaded self-DID entry can't mask real network resolvability. As a result every check was an uncached GET of the VTA's own `did.jsonl`, sent directly or through the resolver sidecar.

When connects keep failing for reasons unrelated to resolvability, the supervisor retries every ≤60 s at the reconnect cap, and every retry fetched the document again. The mediator's own negative cache (the "classic" failure the reconnect loop exists for) and a mediator restart are both such reasons. The first reconnect check straight after a passed gate also fetched the document a second time.

## Change

- Add `readiness::SelfResolutionProbe`. `MessagingConnect::run` creates one and shares it between the gate (`run_gate_with_probe`) and every reconnect check. It records when a **real** network resolution last succeeded and answers from that record for `SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR` = 300 s.
- A real check still goes through `self_did_resolves`: a fresh resolver, built and `stop()`ped per check. So:
  - the preloaded self-DID entry and the long-lived resolver's cache still can't satisfy it;
  - no long-lived network-mode client exists that would need stopping on shutdown;
  - the invariants from the "Mediator connection" section of CLAUDE.md are untouched: nothing new on the startup path, `build_messaging` teardown unchanged, `MIN_HEALTHY_SESSION` unchanged.
- Only successes are remembered. A failed check clears the confirmation, so an unresolvable VTA re-probes on every attempt under the existing backoff.
- The gate's own retries are never short-circuited. Until the gate passes, every attempt is a real resolution.

### Why 300 s

300 s is the default TTL for mutable methods (`did:web`, `did:webvh`) in `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk`, which is the resolver the mediator authenticates us through. The mediator therefore already acts on a copy of our document up to 300 s old, and trusting our own positive observation for the same window adds no staleness that the mediator doesn't already accept.

If the document becomes unresolvable inside the window, the connect's authcrypt check fails and the backoff governs the retry, as before. A window longer than the mediator's cache is where a stale "yes" could hide a real change, so the bound stops there. A test pins the constant.

Net effect: during a run of successful self-resolutions, the probe costs at most one fetch per 300 s instead of one per connect attempt.

## Compatibility

Additive only. `run_gate` and `self_did_network_resolvable` keep their signatures and stateless behaviour, and `SelfResolutionProbe`, `run_gate_with_probe` and `SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR` are new. There is no `!`.

Docs: `docs/02-vta/mediator-connection.md` §2 and the `MediatorReadinessConfig::reconnect` doc comment now describe the window. The CLAUDE.md "Mediator connection" line "re-confirming self-resolution before every attempt" is still true: every attempt still checks, but a recent success now answers the check. I left CLAUDE.md alone.

The SDK half of the same churn (throwaway resolvers per CLI call) is a separate, independent PR.

## Tests

In `messaging::readiness::tests`, driven through an injected probe:
- `consecutive_successful_checks_fetch_once_within_the_window`: 4 checks, 1 real resolution.
- `a_failed_check_is_not_remembered`: failures resolve each time, and the first success then resolves too.

title: fix(vta-service): trust a recent self-resolution instead of re-fetching per connect attempt (#1509)
body:
fix(vta-service): trust a recent self-resolution instead of re-fetching per connect attempt (#1509)

The mediator supervisor re-confirmed that the VTA's own DID resolves over the
network before every connect attempt, and each confirmation built a throwaway
DIDCacheClient and fetched did.jsonl uncached. For a VTA that hosts its own log,
those fetches land on its own unauthenticated routes from its own address and
share the per-IP rate limiter (10 burst, one token per 5 s by default) with
everything else from that address. A run of connects failing for reasons that
have nothing to do with resolvability (the mediator's negative cache, a
mediator restart) spent that budget at one fetch per attempt, and the check
straight after a passed gate fetched the document a second time.

SelfResolutionProbe, owned by MessagingConnect and shared by the gate and every
reconnect, remembers when a real network resolution last succeeded and answers
from that for SELF_RESOLUTION_FRESH_FOR (300 s). Each real check is still a
fresh resolver built and stopped per check, so the preloaded self-DID entry
cannot mask anything and no long-lived socket needs stopping on shutdown. Only
successes are remembered: a failure clears the confirmation and the next
attempt resolves again on the existing backoff.

300 s is the default mutable-method TTL of affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk, the
resolver the mediator authenticates us through, so the mediator already acts on
a copy of our document that old. If the document has become unresolvable
inside the window, the connect's authcrypt check fails and the backoff governs
the retry as before.

run_gate and self_did_network_resolvable keep their signatures and behaviour;
run_gate_with_probe and SelfResolutionProbe are additive.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(webvh): refuse to delete a DID whose hosting server is unregistered
body:
`dids delete` could delete a DID's local record and leave its published log live on the hosting server, without saying so. This PR fixes that for both `pnm did-mgmt dids delete` and the offline `vta did-mgmt dids delete`.

## The bug

In `operations::did_webvh::delete_did_webvh`, the host delete ran only `if let Some(server) = get_server(record.server_id)`. When the DID's server was no longer registered (for example after `servers remove`), `get_server` returned `None`:

- the host delete was skipped,
- `daemon_cleanup_error` stayed `None`,
- the local record was deleted along with the DID's keys, and
- the caller got a plain success.

The host kept serving `did.jsonl`, so the DID still resolved. The local record's mnemonic and the DID's keys were the only credentials that could remove or update that log, and they were deleted with it.

A second gap hid the same symptom when the server *was* registered but the host delete failed. The op reports that case as a partial success through `daemonCleanupError`, which the `vta/webvh/dids/delete/1.0` response schema says a consumer MUST surface. The SDK's `delete_did_webvh` returns `()`, so `pnm` dropped it and printed "WebVH DID deleted".

## The fix

Per VTI R2.1 (Remote-First: no local commit before the remote effect):

- **Server not registered: refused by default.** The check lives in `delete_blockers`, so it runs before anything is written, including credential revocation. It also appears in the offline preview. The refusal is an `AppError::Conflict`, the same typed error as the existing blockers. It arrives as `VtaError::Conflict` on REST, DIDComm and TSP (`details.reason: conflict` on the Trust Task path). The message gives the fix:
  `pnm did-mgmt servers add --id <id> --did <server-did>` (or the offline `vta did-mgmt servers add …`), then retry. For a host that is gone for good it names `vta did-mgmt dids delete <did> --local-only`.
  If the server is unregistered after the check but before the host delete (a race), the op refuses there too, instead of falling back to a silent local delete.
- **`--local-only` (offline `vta` only): explicit opt-in.** For a host that no longer exists, `servers add` cannot succeed because it resolves the server DID. The flag is honoured only when the server is unregistered. For a registered DID it is refused, since the host copy can be deleted there. For a serverless DID it is refused, since there is no host copy. The result's `daemonCleanupError` says the host copy remains, and the CLI prints it.
- **Serverless DIDs:** unchanged.
- **Hosted DID, server registered:** unchanged. `pnm` now calls the new `VtaClient::delete_did_webvh_with_outcome`, which returns the generated `trust_tasks_rs::specs::vta::webvh::dids::delete::v1_0::Response`, and prints `daemonCleanupError` as a warning when the host did not confirm the delete.

`docs/05-design-notes/did-deletion-cascade.md` gains a section on the host copy. It covers why `--local-only` is not the `--force` that note rules out.

### No `!`
Every library change is additive:
- `DeleteDidOptions` (`#[non_exhaustive]`)
- `delete_did_webvh_with`
- `plan_did_deletion_with`
- `VtaClient::delete_did_webvh_with_outcome`
- `MockVta::webvh_host_deletes`

The existing `delete_did_webvh` / `plan_did_deletion` keep their signatures and now refuse the unregistered case. Nothing on the wire changes shape.

## Spec follow-up
The request payload for `vta/webvh/dids/delete/1.0` is generated from the specification with `additionalProperties: false`, so an online `--local-only` needs a `localOnly` member added in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` first, then a `trust-tasks-rs` bump. Until then the opt-in is offline-only.

## Overlap with #1513
#1513 renames `--force` to `--yes` on the same `DeleteDid` / `Delete` clap variants in `vta-service/src/main.rs`. This PR adds one `local_only` field beside it, which will conflict textually. The resolution is mechanical: keep both fields. Once this merges, the `servers delete` notice from #1513 can also point at the refusal.

## Not changed (noted)
- **Server registered but `vta_did` unset.** This still deletes locally and reports it through `daemonCleanupError`, which the response schema allows as a partial success.
- **Host rejects the delete.** Same behaviour. The partial success is now surfaced by `pnm` instead of dropped.

## Tests
New, in `vta-service/tests/mock_vta.rs`, against a real mock VTA and the stub hosting server. The stub now counts accepted `DELETE`s.
- `deleting_a_hosted_did_deletes_its_log_on_the_host`: the host is called, and there is no leftover.
- `deleting_a_did_whose_server_is_unregistered_is_refused_until_it_is_registered_again`: the refusal is a typed `Conflict` naming `servers add --id stub-webvh` and `--local-only`. The host is not called and the record survives. Re-registering the server, then retrying, deletes it.
- `deleting_a_serverless_did_needs_no_host`
- `local_only_is_honoured_only_for_an_unregistered_server_and_says_what_remains`

## Verification
```
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                              ok
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings                   ok
cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest --all-targets -- -D warnings   ok
cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis --all-targets -- -D warnings   ok
cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast   123 targets, 4401 passed, 0 failed
cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast                  62 targets, 1644 passed, 0 failed
```
The runs above were on the parent of #1512. After rebasing onto #1512 (TSP Rev 3, dependency bumps), `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo test -p vta-service --test mock_vta` were re-run and pass.
