title: docs(go): the Go module seeds its own release tag
body:
Corrects guidance I added in #468, which was wrong about an operation that cannot be undone.

`RELEASING.md` told a reader to hand-seed `trust-tasks-go/v<version>` alongside the crate and npm anchors, and `scripts/release-go-pr.sh` said the same in its error message.

## Why it was wrong

`publish-go` does not measure from a prior tag the way `release-go-pr` does. It reads `const Version`, asks whether `trust-tasks-go/v<Version>` exists, and writes it when it does not — so the first push to `main` carrying the module publishes it **and** writes the anchor in one step. `release-go-pr` runs `needs: publish-go`, so by the time it looks there is always a tag.

That is exactly what happened on #468: `publish-go` verified the tree, pushed `trust-tasks-go/v0.1.0` at the merge commit, and `release-go-pr` then correctly reported nothing to release. All six jobs in `publish.yml` were green.

## Why it mattered

Hand-tagging is not merely unnecessary here, it is the riskier path:

- a Go tag **is** the publication — `proxy.golang.org` caches it permanently and it cannot be retracted, only superseded;
- tagging from a local checkout skips the `go build` / `go vet` / `go test` that `publish-go` runs *before* it tags.

So the old instructions pointed at a manual, unverified route to an irreversible action.

## Changes

- `RELEASING.md` — drops the Go tag from the one-time seeding block, adds a short section explaining why there is nothing to seed and why hand-tagging is wrong.
- `scripts/release-go-pr.sh` — the "no tag exists" error now says to re-run `publish-go` rather than to seed by hand, and explains why.
- `CLAUDE.md` — one-line correction to the pointer at RELEASING.md.

Docs only; no behaviour change.

## Verified against the live module

```
$ go get github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go@v0.1.0
go: added ...trust-tasks-go v0.1.0

runtime version:   0.1.0
first delivery:    handled
  response type:   https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1#response
identical resend:  duplicate (§7.2 item 11)
```

title: feat(go): Go bindings and SPEC §7.2 runtime for Trust Tasks
body:
Adds **`trust-tasks-go`**, a third reference implementation alongside `trust-tasks-rs` and `@openvtc/trust-tasks`: a generated payload package for every specification in the registry, plus the hand-written SPEC.md §7.2 consumer pipeline that makes those types mean something.

Scoped to **parity with the TypeScript package** — generated types, the §7.2 pipeline, conformance tests, drift CI and release automation. No transport bindings; those are separate work.

## What is here

| | |
|---|---|
| `scripts/build-go-bindings.mjs` | 985 lines. Emits one self-contained Go package per schema; gofmts its own output |
| `trust-tasks-go/specs/**` | 509 generated packages, 66k lines |
| `trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/**` | 3,840 lines hand-written: envelope, §7.2 pipeline, §8.3/§8.5 codes, canonicalization, freshness, replay guard, transport seam |
| `trust-tasks-go/smoke/` | drives a *generated* package through the real pipeline — the counterpart of `npm run smoke` |
| `.github/workflows/go.yml` | drift, build+vet+gofmt, test |
| `scripts/release-go-pr.sh` + `publish-go` / `release-go-pr` | the publishing half |

79 tests, mirroring the TypeScript suite case for case.

## Cross-language conformance

`npm run check-bindings` is now **three-way**. All 442 specifications checked across Rust, TypeScript and Go — 863 policy blocks and 863 schema documents, zero disagreements:

```
Bindings conformance: 442 specifications checked against 442 TypeScript,
437 Rust and 442 Go modules — all agree.
```

The Go generator deliberately **re-implements** the `$ref` inliner and the front-matter policy derivation rather than importing the TypeScript ones. Sharing them would reduce the comparison to asserting a resolver agrees with itself — the property that already held while two defects shipped (#174, #215). Its file header says so; please don't DRY it up in review.

Verified by tampering: flipping a policy flag and altering the shipped schema text both fail the check and name both sides.

## Design decisions worth reviewing

**Follows Rust, not TypeScript, on hoisting.** Go is nominally typed, so collapsing `Ext` into one shared package would merge type identities the way #283 declined for Rust. Each generated package is self-contained.

**One Go package is one *directory*, not one file.** TypeScript gives `auth/_shared/0.1/session.ts` and `tokens.ts` separate namespaces and both declare `Ext`; side by side in Go that is a redeclaration error. So every schema gets its own directory. Also: `_shared` and `_framework` become `shared` and `framework`, because the go command ignores directories starting with `_` — a package under one would be generated, committed and silently unreachable.

**Absent is not empty.** Optional members are pointers, *including slices and maps*. `omitempty` on a plain slice drops an empty one from the wire, collapsing "present and empty" into "absent" — which `acl`'s `allowedKeys` documents as re-creating "the empty-means-unrestricted class of privilege-escalation defect this family's conventions exist to prevent". Rust spells this `Option<Vec<T>>` and TypeScript `scopes?: string[]`; a bare Go slice was the only one of the three that could not say it. `*[]string` is ugly and deliberate; `smoke` pins it.

**Go 1.22 floor, proven not asserted.** The build/test matrix pins the `go` directive value explicitly as well as `stable`, so a 1.25-ism can't creep in unnoticed. Verified locally against a real 1.22 toolchain.

**`PayloadPolicy` and `Checks` are required options**, and an unset one is an error rather than a default. Both have a Go zero value that reads as "skip it", and defaulting to skipping would silently reproduce the defects they exist to remove.

## Publishing, and how it fits the existing cycle

A Go module is published by pushing a `trust-tasks-go/vX.Y.Z` tag — no registry account, no token, no OIDC exchange. `publish-go` / `release-go-pr` mirror the existing npm half.

It coexists with release-plz cleanly:

- No crate is named `trust-tasks-go`, and `release-plz.toml` sets no `git_tag_name`, so release-plz uses its default `{{package}}-v{{version}}`. The Go tag's **slash** matches none of the 338 existing `<crate>-v*` or `trust-tasks-ts-v*` tags.
- The slash is mandated by the go tooling for a subdirectory module, and as a side effect puts Go tags in their own `refs/tags/trust-tasks-go/` namespace.
- Each Release PR force-pushes its own branch — release-plz's own, `release-ts`, `release-go`. No shared state.

### ⚠️ One manual step after merge

`trust-tasks-go/v*` has **no anchor tag yet** (the crate and npm anchors already exist). `release-go-pr` will fail loudly with *"No trust-tasks-go/v\* tag exists"* — by design — until it is seeded. Seed it on the merge commit:

```bash
git switch main && git pull
git tag -s trust-tasks-go/v0.1.0 -m "trust-tasks-go 0.1.0"
git push origin trust-tasks-go/v0.1.0
```

For Go that tag **is** the publication, not just an anchor — unlike the inert `trust-tasks-ts-v*` tags. And it cannot be retracted: `proxy.golang.org` caches a tag permanently by design, so tag only a tree you mean to ship. `publish-go` builds, vets and tests before tagging for that reason.

## Checks run locally

- `npm run build-go-bindings` — idempotent, gofmt-clean
- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test -race ./...` — clean across 509 packages
- `npm run check-bindings` — 442 specs, three languages, all agree
- `npm run validate` — 442 specs, 72 shared schemas
- `npm test` in `trust-tasks-ts` — 79 pass, unchanged

title: build(deps): take vta-sdk 0.39, on a single sdk node
body:
VTI published `vta-sdk 0.39.0` — a major: `verify_trust_task_proof_with` became
generic over the payload, and `KeyType` gained ML-DSA variants.

## Two edges had to move, and this manifest named both in advance

- **`did-git-sign` 0.4.10 → 0.4.11.** 0.4.10 requires `vta-sdk ^0.38`, so
  raising this workspace's pin resolved two sdk copies. VGI published 0.4.11
  against `^0.39` (VGI #55, #56) to clear it. The floor names the patch for the
  reason already recorded here: a bare `"0.4"` lets a clean checkout resolve
  back to a release that reintroduces the duplicate, and 0.4.10 is now such a
  release.
- **`vta-service` 0.27 → 0.29**, the `MockVta` dev-dependency. This is the edge
  this file warns "gets forgotten", and it was: bumping `did-git-sign` alone
  left the second sdk in place, held by `vta-service` 0.27 and the eleven VTI
  crates in its closure. It took `cargo tree -d` to see that — the
  `did-git-sign` bump on its own looked like it had worked.

`cargo tree -i vta-sdk` now resolves a single 0.39.0 node, and `cargo tree -d`
reports no duplicate `vta-sdk`, `trust-tasks-rs`, `vti-common` or `vta-service`.

## One source change

`KeyType` is `#[non_exhaustive]` and gained ML-DSA variants, so
`secret_from_vta_response`'s match stopped being exhaustive. The per-variant
`P256` arm is now a catch-all that names whatever it refused: this function
converts a VTA key into a TDK `Secret`, and a key type TDK has no `Secret` for
is unsupported here whatever it is called. Enumerating would mean editing it
every time the SDK learns a key type, to keep saying the same thing.

## The trust-tasks floor follows the sdk

0.39 declares `trust-tasks-rs ^0.20.7` where 0.38 declared `^0.20.4`, so the
floor here moves to 0.20.7 by this file's own rule: a floor below what the sdk
requires is a floor that does nothing. `trust-tasks-capability-client` moves
with it, for the reason stated beside it — a copy left on an older trust-tasks
is a second semver-incompatible `trust-tasks-rs` whose types do not unify.

title: fix(tsp)!: one transport for TSP, and it must carry a mediator
body:
## The report

`pnm did-mgmt dids create --server dids` against a did-host advertising `#tsp` fails instantly:

```
✗ Protocol error: trust task failed [internalError]: internal error: the consumer
  could not complete this task; the request itself was accepted
```

and in the VTA's log:

```
ERROR vta_service::trust_tasks::helpers: trust task failed with an internal error
  cause=bad gateway: `did:webvh:Qmbxds…:dids.ic3.dev` could not be reached over TSP:
  Config error: No Mediator is configured for this Profile
```

The preceding `webvh/servers/domains/0.1` call in the same session succeeded, which is what makes this confusing to read: the VTA answers over TSP perfectly well.

## Root cause

The VTA held **two `ATMProfile`s for its own DID**, and the outbound path had the wrong one.

| built in | mediator | used by |
|---|---|---|
| `server::init_auth` → `AppState.tsp_profile` | **`None`** | vault TSP unseal, step-up push, and — since #1482/#1483 — the outbound seam |
| `messaging::service::build_messaging` → `VtaMessaging.profile` | `Some(mediator)` | `handle_tsp`, which seals inbound replies |

The mediator-less one dates to #594, built on the reasoning — written into the comment — that unsealing reads the decryption key from the ATM's secrets resolver and "needs no mediator."

**That reasoning is false.** Every TSP entry point in `affinidi-messaging-sdk` resolves the mediator off the profile handed to it:

- `TspOps::pack` → `ATMProfile::dids()`
- `TspOps::unpack_bytes` → `ATMProfile::dids()` (to check the envelope's intended receiver)
- `TspOps::send_raw` → `dids()` **and** `get_mediator_rest_endpoint()`

All three answer `ConfigError("No Mediator is configured for this Profile")` without one, *before any I/O*. So that profile could neither send **nor** unseal — the vault `tsp-message` path it was built for had never worked either. It is not a receive-only profile; it is a non-functional one.

It stayed invisible because a mediator-less profile is *selectable*: right type, registers on an ATM without complaint, fails only when asked to do work. #1482 (reply correlation in the spine) and #1483 (the webvh transport selector) then made the outbound seam able to *choose* TSP, it reached for the nearest profile-shaped thing in `AppState`, and every TSP send this VTA attempted died inside the SDK.

## The fix: one transport

New `messaging::tsp_transport::TspTransport` — the ATM, the profile registered on it, and the mediator **read off that profile**. `TspTransport::new` calls `dids()` and returns `None` when the profile cannot route, so a mediator-less profile cannot become a transport and the defect is no longer expressible.

| before | after |
|---|---|
| `handle_tsp` took `mediator_did` down a parameter chain from `run_inbound_loop`, past a DIDComm arm that discarded it | uses the session transport `build_messaging` builds once; the param is gone from all three functions |
| `outbound::TspSender` read the mediator from `AppConfig` — a second source, unchecked against the first | holds a `TspTransport`; no config read |
| `step_up::try_push_over_tsp` took it from a caller that computed it for the *DIDComm* fallback | takes the transport; `approver_mediator` still gates whether to push |
| `trust_tasks::vault` passed an ATM and a profile from different places | passes one `TspTransport`, so the pair cannot be mismatched |
| three hand-rolled `send_routed([mediator, recipient])` call sites | one `TspTransport::send_to` |

`AppState.tsp_profile` is removed; `AppState::tsp_transport()` is the only door. `None` means no live mediator session, which drops TSP from transport *selection* rather than choosing it and then failing to send — so the peer is reached over its next-preferred protocol instead.

`build_messaging` builds the session transport right after `profile_add` and returns `Err` (after `graceful_shutdown`, per the teardown invariant) if the profile it just registered cannot route. A session that can receive but not answer is refused at connect.

### What deliberately did *not* consolidate

The VTA keeps **two ATMs**, and that is correct. `AppState.atm` is built in `init_auth` with no socket and no mediator; the messaging ATM exists only while a session is up and is rebuilt on every reconnect. Vault release, proxy-login and the DIDComm-envelope auth path pack and unpack through `AppState.atm` with no profile at all, and must keep working on a REST-only VTA and whenever a session is down. Folding them together would tie those paths to the mediator's uptime. Two ATMs with different lifetimes was never the defect — two *profiles*, one of which could not work, was.

## Why nothing caught it

`MockVta::start_with_transports` reproduced the same split: it ran the inbound loop but left the bridge a placeholder and built its own mediator-less profile, exactly as `init_auth` did. A harness that only ever answers cannot show that the initiating half is broken.

It now publishes the wiring the way `MessagingConnect::connect_once` does, and three tests hold the line:

- **`the_vta_can_initiate_a_tsp_send_not_only_answer_one`** — a real routed send through the embedded test mediator. Falsified: with the old profile put back it fails with `Some(ConfigError("No Mediator is configured for this Profile"))`, the reported error verbatim.
- **`tsp_is_not_offered_before_a_mediator_session_exists`** — selection follows the live session, not config.
- **`atm_profile_mediator_census`** — fails the build on any `ATMProfile::new(…, None)` under `vta-service/src`, with an empty allowlist. Falsified against `status.rs`. Ungated, so it runs in the default CI workspace job.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **122 targets, 4351 tests, 0 failures**
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- Reduced feature sets CI runs: `--features rest` (no didcomm, no tsp), `--features setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis` (tsp without didcomm), `--features tee,rest,didcomm`, `--features tsp`, `--features transport-harness` — all clean

## Breaking changes

`vta-service` public API:

- `AppState.tsp_profile` removed — use `AppState::tsp_transport()`
- `DIDCommBridge::set_messaging` takes the session's `Arc<ATMProfile>`
- `VtaMessaging` gains a `tsp` field under the `tsp` feature
- `run_inbound_loop` and `operations::vault::upsert::unseal_tsp_secret` drop arguments now read from the profile
- `operations::outbound::TspSender` no longer borrows, so it has no lifetime parameter

No wire-format or configuration change; operators need do nothing.

title: fix(tsp)!: one transport for TSP, and it must carry a mediator (#1507)
body:
fix(tsp)!: one transport for TSP, and it must carry a mediator (#1507)

`pnm did-mgmt dids create` against a did-host advertising `#tsp` failed
instantly with `trust task failed [internalError]`, and in the VTA's log:

    bad gateway: `did:webvh:...:dids.ic3.dev` could not be reached over TSP:
    Config error: No Mediator is configured for this Profile

The VTA held two `ATMProfile`s for its own DID. `server::init_auth` built one
with **no mediator** and parked it in `AppState.tsp_profile`, reasoning that
unsealing a TSP envelope reads the decryption key from the ATM's secrets
resolver and so needs no route. `messaging::service::build_messaging` built the
mediator-bearing one and kept it inside `VtaMessaging`, where only the inbound
loop could see it.

That reasoning is false. Every TSP entry point in the messaging SDK resolves the
mediator off the profile handed to it: `TspOps::pack` and `unpack_bytes` call
`ATMProfile::dids()`, and `send_raw` calls it alongside
`get_mediator_rest_endpoint()`. All three answer `ConfigError("No Mediator is
configured for this Profile")` without one, before any I/O — so that profile
could neither send *nor* unseal, and the vault `tsp-message` path it was built
for had never worked either.

It stayed invisible because a mediator-less profile is selectable: right type,
registers on an ATM without complaint, fails only when asked to do work. The VTA
answered TSP correctly throughout, because `handle_tsp` seals replies on the
other profile. When #1482/#1483 taught the outbound seam to *initiate* over TSP,
it sealed on the profile `AppState` held, and every TSP send died inside the SDK.

Consolidated onto one type, `messaging::tsp_transport::TspTransport`: the ATM,
the profile registered on it, and the mediator read off that profile. Its
constructor calls `dids()`, so a mediator-less profile cannot become a transport
and the defect is no longer expressible.

- `handle_tsp` uses the session transport `build_messaging` now builds, so
  `mediator_did` leaves `run_inbound_loop`, `handle_inbound` and `handle_tsp` —
  it was threaded past a DIDComm arm that discarded it. A session whose profile
  cannot route fails the connect instead of coming up able to receive and not to
  answer.
- `outbound::TspSender` holds a `TspTransport` instead of a mediator copied out
  of `AppConfig`: one fact, one source, nothing to disagree.
- `step_up::try_push_over_tsp` drops its `mediator_did` argument; the caller's
  `approver_mediator` still gates whether a push happens and still picks the
  DIDComm fallback's route.
- `operations::vault::upsert::unseal_tsp_secret` takes the transport rather than
  an ATM and a profile that came from different places.
- `AppState.tsp_profile` is removed. `AppState::tsp_transport()` is the only way
  in, and `None` means no live mediator session — which drops TSP from transport
  selection rather than choosing it and then failing to send.

The two ATMs stay, and that is deliberate. `AppState.atm` has no socket and no
mediator by design: vault release, proxy-login and the DIDComm-envelope auth path
pack and unpack through it with no profile at all, and must keep working on a
REST-only VTA and while a session is down. Two ATMs with different lifetimes was
never the defect; two profiles, one of which could not work, was.

Nothing caught this because `MockVta::start_with_transports` reproduced the same
split — it ran the inbound loop but left the bridge a placeholder and built its
own mediator-less profile, so it could only ever answer. It now publishes the
wiring the way `MessagingConnect::connect_once` does, and three tests hold the
line:

- `the_vta_can_initiate_a_tsp_send_not_only_answer_one` drives a real routed send
  through the embedded mediator, and reproduces the reported error verbatim when
  the old profile is put back;
- `tsp_is_not_offered_before_a_mediator_session_exists` pins selection to the
  live session rather than to config;
- `atm_profile_mediator_census` fails the build on any `ATMProfile::new(...,
  None)` under `vta-service/src`, with an empty allowlist.

BREAKING CHANGE: `AppState.tsp_profile` is removed — use
`AppState::tsp_transport()`. `DIDCommBridge::set_messaging` takes the session's
`Arc<ATMProfile>`; `VtaMessaging` gains a `tsp` field under the `tsp` feature;

title: build(deps): take vta-sdk 0.39, so OpenVTC can follow without a duplicate
body:
VTI published `vta-sdk 0.39.0`, a major: `verify_trust_task_proof_with` became
generic over the payload, and `KeyType` gained ML-DSA variants.

While this line declared `^0.38`, **OpenVTC could not move.** It consumes
`did-git-sign`, so raising its own pin resolved *two* sdk copies — 0.38.2 for
this crate and 0.39.0 for itself. That is the state OpenVTC's manifest records
having escaped "for the first time since 0.35", after the obligation here had
blocked six consecutive minors (0.23, 0.25, 0.27, 0.31, 0.32, 0.34).

This line's own note named the job: *"It is one row here today; it will be two
in OpenVTC until that move happens, and that is the thing to fix next."* This is
that move.

## It compiled unchanged

No source edit was needed. Neither breaking change in 0.39 touches this
workspace: nothing here calls `verify_trust_task_proof_with`, and nothing
matches on `KeyType` (OpenVTC did, and needed a catch-all arm). The pin was the
whole of it.

Verified rather than assumed: `cargo tree -i vta-sdk` resolves a **single**
0.39.0 node, and `cargo tree -d` shows no sdk row at all. `fmt`, `clippy
--workspace --all-targets -D warnings` and the full test suite are green.

## Why a duplicate is not merely untidy

While the last one lasted it cost a `cargo tree -d` row rather than a build
failure, for a narrow reason: OpenVTC uses `did_git_sign::{config, init}` only,
so no sdk type crosses that boundary. One new import turns it into a type error,
because `vti-common` re-exports `vta_sdk::acl` types that cannot unify across
copies. Keeping this line current is what keeps that trap closed.

title: feat(keys): derive ML-DSA keys from the BIP-32 chain
body:
`Bip32Extension` gains `derive_ml_dsa_44` and `derive_ml_dsa_65`, and the five
sites that refused post-quantum derivation now do it: key creation, both export
paths, and the offline `vta keys secrets` CLI. This is what stands between "a
`KeyRecord` can carry a post-quantum key" and "a VTA can mint one".

## Domain separation is the whole of it

`derive_ed25519` hands the SLIP-0010 output straight to the key constructor, and
FIPS 204 KeyGen takes a 32-byte seed — so the obvious implementation lines up,
compiles, and is wrong: **the ML-DSA seed would equal the Ed25519 private key at
the same path**, and compromising either would yield the other. Both values are
32 bytes, which is exactly why it reads as correct.

`derive_p256` already solved this, and these follow its construction exactly —
HMAC-SHA512 over the derived signing key and chain code, keyed by a label, first
32 bytes taken. **The label differs per parameter set**, because ML-DSA-44 and
ML-DSA-65 are different algorithms and a holder of one must not be able to
reconstruct the other.

This is not theoretical. I built the naive version first and
`ml_dsa_seed_is_independent_of_the_ed25519_key_at_the_same_path` fails against
it with exactly that message. `the_two_ml_dsa_parameter_sets_get_independent_seeds`
covers the second half, and `ml_dsa_derivation_is_deterministic` the property
that makes a derived key recoverable from the mnemonic at all.

Simpler than P-256 in one respect: xi is 32 arbitrary bytes with no group-order
constraint, so there is no reduction and no retry loop.

The shared helper exists because the two derivations differ only in the label,
and a second copy is how they would eventually disagree about how a seed is
produced — which is unrecoverable rather than merely wrong, since the key cannot
be re-derived afterwards.

## Internal keys still refuse, and the comment now says why

Not blocked on cryptography any more — `affinidi_crypto::ml_dsa` signs and this
change derives. What is missing is a **decision**.

An internal key is deliberately the opposite of a derived one: CSPRNG-generated,
no derivation path, absent from the mnemonic, so losing the keyspace loses it and
everything it authorises. Whether a VTA should hold an *unrecoverable*
post-quantum signing key is a question about that trade, and it should not be
inherited from a change whose subject was derivation. The stale comment claiming
ML-DSA was blocked on derivation is corrected.

## One feature flag

Enables `affinidi-secrets-resolver`'s `ml-dsa` feature, which nothing in this
workspace had turned on — so `Secret::generate_ml_dsa_44` was not compiled here
at all.

## Checks

121 test suites green under `--no-fail-fast` (the CI invocation), clippy clean
under `-D warnings`, rustfmt clean. No version field edited, no changelog file
added.

significance_reasons: Normative requirement language changed

title: vti-rooms-v0.2.5
body:
### Added

- **rooms**: The wire types name the task they are the payload of ([#1498](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1498))

Groundwork for keying dispatch on the **type** rather than on a URI written out
  at the registration site. `trust_tasks_rs::Payload` is the framework's statement
  that a Rust type *is* the payload of a task URI; with it, a dispatcher derives
  routing, `unsupportedType`-vs-`unsupportedVersion`, and its own served-URI list
  from the registrations themselves.

  The URI stops being an argument someone has to supply correctly. That matters
  here because this repo has already shipped the bug that a string-keyed router
  invites: `rooms/records/curate` was dispatched and named in neither URI list, so
  every version hint the service emitted was wrong about it. The list and the
  router were two descriptions of one fact, and they disagreed.

### Added - **keys**: ML-DSA key types, and one codec table instead of two ([#1502](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1502)) - **vtc**: Verify a Trust Task's proof in the spine, where the bytes still exist ([#1501](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1501)) * feat(vtc): verify a Trust Task's proof in the spine, where the bytes still exist A proof covers the document as it was **sent**. `rooms/*` handlers verified it themselves, from the `TrustTask` they were handed — which works only while they are handed the document verbatim. They cannot keep doing that. Keying dispatch on the payload type hands a handler `TrustTask

`, and re-deriving the signed bytes from a parsed payload is sound only if `P` round-trips losslessly. None does: parse a document into a type that does not know one of its members and the member is gone, so the canonicalisation differs and a valid proof is refused. Pinned by `vta-sdk/tests/typed_proof_verify.rs`. So verification moves to `dispatch_trust_task_core`, which is the last point at which the received bytes exist, and the verified signer travels on `JoinAuthCtx`.

title: fix(didcomm): send Trust Tasks in the binding envelope, not typed as the task
body:
The last hand-rolled carriage here. Four sends typed their DIDComm message with
the **task URI** — `Message::build(id, JOIN_REQUEST_SUBMIT_TYPE, …)` — where the
binding says the type is `TRUST_TASK_ENVELOPE_TYPE` with the task inside. It
worked only because `vtc-service` keeps a router keyed on task URIs: the same
private dialect this workspace spent the week removing from TSP, and the same
one that made the TSP outage silent rather than loud.

VTI #1497 made the envelope route reachable on the receiving side, so the
receiver has been ready; the sender was not.

## Two of them were not even sending documents

`members/self-remove` and `members/vmc` sent a **bare payload**. That reached a
VTC handler which bypasses its dispatch spine entirely, so those replies were
never signed and a refusal came back as a DIDComm problem-report rather than a
framework error document — "no answer this service gave was evidence of
anything", in the words of the VTC's own commit that fixed the same thing for
its other verbs.

Both now build a document through `trust_task_doc::build_value`.

## Why the replies keep working

Checked rather than assumed, because this is the half that breaks silently:

- `members/vmc`: the bare-body handler replies `MEMBER_VMC_RESPONSE_TYPE`, and
  that constant is exactly `MEMBER_VMC_TYPE#response` — which is what the
  spine's `success_response` produces. `message_dispatch`'s arm for it keeps
  matching, unchanged.
- `members/self-remove`: nothing in this crate routes a reply to it. It is
  fire-and-forget, so there is nothing to keep matching.
- `join-requests/submit` and `status`: already sent documents, and both paths
  reach the same handler through `dispatch_trust_task_core`, so the reply is
  byte-identical either way.

The message id stays the document id on the submit path. That is what makes the
DIDComm and TSP threading conventions coincide, and it is load-bearing — see
`submit_join_request`'s own docs.

## What this does not do

It does not let `vtc-service` delete its bare-body handlers. Those must stay
until no deployed client sends the old shape; sender first, receiver second.
Reversing that order is precisely what turned a binding change into an outage
last week.

title: feat(keys)!: ML-DSA key types, and one codec table instead of two
body:
`vta_sdk::keys::KeyType` gains `MlDsa44` and `MlDsa65`, and is marked
`#[non_exhaustive]`. **The attribute is the breaking part** — an exhaustive
`match` in a consumer stops compiling — and it is deliberate: this enum will
keep growing, and RELEASING.md's own advice is that for such a type the
attribute beats remembering the `!` on every future addition.

## Two parameter sets, on purpose

W3C Quantum-Resistant Cryptosuites defines Data Integrity suites only for
**ML-DSA-44**; TSP Rev 3 §8.1 mandates **ML-DSA-65**. The set is chosen by
whatever consumes the key, never by the holder, so they are not redundant. The
doc comments say so, because the instinct on seeing two adjacent parameter sets
is to delete one.

## Requires `trust-tasks-rs` 0.20.7

That release carries the widened `keys/_shared/0.1` `keyType` enumeration
(dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#463). Without it the VTA emits a `keyType` the published
schema does not list and then **rejects its own response** at the dispatch
spine — a 500 on an operation that otherwise succeeded.
`a_post_quantum_key_record_validates_against_the_published_schema` is the check
that the whole four-repository chain actually arrived.

## The codec table moved, and that is the interesting part

Widening the enum broke `vta-keys`' private copy of the multicodec table, which
is how the duplicate finally got removed.

The obvious fix — a wildcard arm — would have been a **defect**. A codec table's
wildcard cannot produce a *correct* prefix, only a wrong one, and a multibase
string under a wrong prefix round-trips perfectly inside this workspace and
decodes as the wrong algorithm everywhere else.

The second obvious fix — make the encoders fallible — would have touched 22 call
sites. Neither was needed. `#[non_exhaustive]` binds *other* crates, so the
table now lives beside the enum in `vta-sdk` as `multicodec_public` /
`multicodec_private`, where the match is genuinely exhaustive and a new
`KeyType` is a compile error until it is given a codec. `vta-keys` delegates,
the encoders stay infallible, no call site moved, and there is one table.

## Seven wildcard arms, and they do not all mean the same thing

**Six refuse.** Four BIP-32 derivation sites and two internal-key sites: there
is no `derive_ml_dsa` yet, and a fallback would mint a key of another algorithm
wearing an ML-DSA label. FIPS 204 KeyGen takes a 32-byte seed, so the chain
*can* produce one — the `-priv-seed` codecs exist for exactly that — but the
derivation belongs beside its siblings in `ExtendedSigningKey`, not inlined at
six call sites. That is the next piece of work.

**One counts.** `status.rs` tallies keys by type, so a wildcard that merely fell
through would leave the breakdown failing to add up to `total_keys` — with the
missing keys being precisely the new ones nobody is looking for yet. It gets an
`other` bucket that prints when non-zero.

## Checks

121 test suites green under `--no-fail-fast` (the CI invocation), clippy clean
under `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all --check` clean. No version field edited
and no changelog file added.

title: refactor(core): build a Trust Task document in one place, not three
body:
`join::build_trust_task_document`, `personhood::build_document` and
`vetting::wire::document` were the same function three times. They differed only
in whether they returned a `Value` or a `TrustTask<Value>`; parsing the type URI
and setting `issuer`, `recipient` and `issuedAt` was identical in all three.

`join.rs` named the hazard in a comment while the second copy was being written:

> a second verb writing its own copy is how one of them ends up subtly different

There were three by the time this landed, and the difference they guard against
is not theoretical. A document missing `issuedAt` is refused by a peer enforcing
framework §7.3 item 17; one missing `recipient` is refused under §7.2 item 5b.
Neither refusal names the missing field on the sender's side — it arrives as a
`malformedRequest`, or as nothing at all.

## The proof is an unused import

Delegating left `trust_tasks_rs::TrustTask` unused in both `join.rs` and
`personhood.rs`: **neither file constructs a Trust Task any more.** That is a
better demonstration than any assertion that there is one builder now, and it is
the same signal #1478 used when `webvh_didcomm` stopped hand-rolling its
carriage.

## What is in the module and what is not

The envelope — the fields every document carries regardless of verb. Not the
payload, not the proof, not the carriage: a document is addressed and dated
here, signed by whoever owns the key, and wrapped by whichever binding carries
it.

`document_id` stays a parameter rather than being minted inside, because the
caller often needs it to correlate a reply — and on the DIDComm path the same id
is the message id, which is what makes the two transports' reply threading agree
(`join::submit_join_request`).

Three tests: every framework-checked field is present, asserted one at a time so
the failure names which is missing and what refuses it; the two entry points
describe the same document, which is precisely the difference three copies were
free to develop; and a malformed type URI fails at build time rather than on the
wire.

## Not in this change

Two things the wider refactor still wants here, both wire-affecting and both
needing a sequence rather than an edit:

- `members/self-remove` and `members/vmc` still send a **bare body** typed with
  the task URI, so the VTC answers them from handlers that bypass its dispatch
  spine — those replies are never signed and never produce framework error
  documents. Fixing it means sending a document in the binding envelope (which
  VTI #1497 made reachable) and checking the reply routing against a live round
  trip, because the two paths reply with different shapes.
- The hand-written wire types cannot simply become re-exports of the generated
  ones: those use newtypes, `NonZeroU64` and `#[non_exhaustive]`, so the swap is
  a published API break that ripples across the repo boundary. `vti-rooms`
  records a deliberate decision not to adopt them for exactly this reason.

title: refactor(core): build a Trust Task document in one place, not three (#330)
body:
refactor(core): build a Trust Task document in one place, not three (#330)

* fix(didcomm): make a forgotten routing prefix fail a test, not a deployment

An inbound message whose `type` the gate does not match is **dropped** — a
`debug!` line and nothing else. Not refused: dropped. The sender gets no error,
no problem-report, and nothing but a wait that never ends.

So a branch added to `process_inbound_message` without a matching prefix in
`OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` is a verb that fails totally and silently. That is
not hypothetical — it is the bug fixed last week: `send_capability_document`
sent the binding envelope, `message_dispatch` had a branch for exactly that
type, and every reply was dropped in between. Nothing was red; the symptom was
capability writes that appeared to go unacknowledged.

The gate and the dispatcher are two descriptions of one fact — which types this
client handles — and two descriptions agree until someone edits one.
`openvtc/tests/inbound_gate_census.rs` is the check that they still do.

## `routes_inbound_type`, and the near-miss that shaped it

The predicate is exposed rather than left as a raw pattern, so a caller asks the
gate instead of recompiling the regex and asking a copy — the same duplication
the pattern keeps producing.

Its first version asked only `CATCH_ALL`, and the census immediately reported
`trust-ping/2.0/ping-response` as dropped. It is not: `classify_inbound` returns
on both trust-ping types *before* consulting the pattern. Taken at face value
that finding would have sent someone to widen a regex that was never the
problem, which is worse than no census at all. The predicate now mirrors
`classify_inbound`'s admission order exactly.

## Why a hand-written list

The honest fix is a registry the gate is *derived* from, so the two cannot
differ — the direction `vtc-service` took for `rooms/*`, where
`registered_uris()` is the served list rather than a copy of one (VTI #1503).

`process_inbound_message` cannot go there yet. It threads `&mut Config` and
`&mut InboundEffects` through every arm, and a type-keyed dispatcher needs
handler futures that are `'static`, so the change is to this app's state model
rather than to its routing — a much larger and riskier piece of work, and a
different one.

Until then the list is the seam, and it is written out on purpose: a list
generated from the branches would answer "yes" by construction and prove
nothing. What is being caught is exactly "someone added a branch and did not
tell the gate".

Two supporting tests: every `trust-task-error` version passes the gate, not just
the current one (a peer on another framework version would otherwise have its
refusals silently dropped, which reads as a request that was never answered);
and the gate still refuses what this client does not route, so the census cannot
be satisfied by a pattern that matches the world.

title: feat(tsp)!: the Trust Tasks TSP binding speaks spec Rev 3
body:
`affinidi-tsp` 0.1 → 0.2. Rev 3 and Rev 2 **do not interoperate in either
direction**, so a consumer of this binding moves with its peers or goes silent
— hence the `!`.

## The API change is one idea, applied four times

HPKE-**Base** replaces HPKE-Auth, and Base does not use the sender's KEM key.
So `pack`, `pack_nested`, `pack_routed` and `unpack` each lost their
sender-encryption-key argument: packing now needs only the sender's *signing*
secret. Nothing else in `pack.rs` moved.

`next_hop` also now takes the whole `UnpackedMessage` rather than a payload
slice, because Rev 3 carries the route in the payload frame.

## Two tests asserted a leak that Rev 3 closes

`nested_roundtrip_through_intermediary` and `routed_roundtrips_through_a_relay`
checked that a keys-free `MetaEnvelope::parse` reports `Nested` / `Routed`.
That was true in Rev 2, which carried the message type in the **cleartext**
envelope — so any relay could tell a nested message from a direct one without
holding a key.

Rev 3 encrypts it. `MetaEnvelope::message_type` is documented as a keys-free
placeholder that always reads `Direct`, and a relay needing the real kind must
open the message. Both tests now assert that, and say why — the old assertion
was asserting the leak, and the nested test's own comment ("bob's identity
stays hidden from anyone but the intermediary") is better served by the new
behaviour than by the one it was checking.

## The dependency refresh, and why it is in the same commit

Bumping `affinidi-tsp` alone does not build. It pulls `affinidi-did-common`
0.4, and this workspace's lockfile held a stale patch of nearly every
`affinidi-*` crate — several pinned down by dev-dependencies that had not moved
in a long time:

| crate | dev-dependency | from | to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | `affinidi-tdk` | 0.7 | 0.15 |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | `affinidi-messaging-sdk` | 0.18 | 0.25 |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` | 0.2 | 0.8 |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | `affinidi-did-common` | 0.3 | 0.4 |

Those were holding `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` at 0.8.13 when 0.8.37 was
current, which kept the `affinidi-did-common` 0.3 line alive beside 0.4. With
them moved the family floats to current patches and **no `affinidi-*` crate is
duplicated in the graph any more** — the property that actually matters, since
two `affinidi-tsp` nodes would mean two TSP revisions in one binary.

Worth recording because the diagnosis was wrong twice before it was right: the
compile error is `JWK::new` / `OctectParams::new` not found *inside*
`affinidi-did-common`, which reads as "did-common is broken" and is not — it
was an `affinidi-crypto` patch old enough to predate those constructors.

## Why now

This unblocks `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`, which cannot cut over to Rev 3
while this binding still resolves `affinidi-tsp` 0.1 beside the 0.2 its own
dependencies pull. VTI's migration note recorded the chain as three repositories;
it is four, and this is the missing one.

## Checks

44 test suites green under `--no-fail-fast`, clippy clean under `-D warnings`,
`cargo fmt --all --check` clean.

title: fix(didcomm): make a forgotten routing prefix fail a test, not a deployment
body:
An inbound message whose `type` the gate does not match is **dropped** — a
`debug!` line and nothing else. Not refused: dropped. The sender gets no error,
no problem-report, and nothing but a wait that never ends.

So a branch added to `process_inbound_message` without a matching prefix in
`OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` is a verb that fails totally and silently. That is
not hypothetical — it is the bug fixed last week: `send_capability_document`
sent the binding envelope, `message_dispatch` had a branch for exactly that
type, and every reply was dropped in between. Nothing was red; the symptom was
capability writes that appeared to go unacknowledged.

The gate and the dispatcher are two descriptions of one fact — which types this
client handles — and two descriptions agree until someone edits one.
`openvtc/tests/inbound_gate_census.rs` is the check that they still do.

## `routes_inbound_type`, and the near-miss that shaped it

The predicate is exposed rather than left as a raw pattern, so a caller asks the
gate instead of recompiling the regex and asking a copy — the same duplication
the pattern keeps producing.

Its first version asked only `CATCH_ALL`, and the census immediately reported
`trust-ping/2.0/ping-response` as dropped. It is not: `classify_inbound` returns
on both trust-ping types *before* consulting the pattern. Taken at face value
that finding would have sent someone to widen a regex that was never the
problem, which is worse than no census at all. The predicate now mirrors
`classify_inbound`'s admission order exactly.

## Why a hand-written list

The honest fix is a registry the gate is *derived* from, so the two cannot
differ — the direction `vtc-service` took for `rooms/*`, where
`registered_uris()` is the served list rather than a copy of one (VTI #1503).

`process_inbound_message` cannot go there yet. It threads `&mut Config` and
`&mut InboundEffects` through every arm, and a type-keyed dispatcher needs
handler futures that are `'static`, so the change is to this app's state model
rather than to its routing — a much larger and riskier piece of work, and a
different one.

Until then the list is the seam, and it is written out on purpose: a list
generated from the branches would answer "yes" by construction and prove
nothing. What is being caught is exactly "someone added a branch and did not
tell the gate".

Two supporting tests: every `trust-task-error` version passes the gate, not just
the current one (a peer on another framework version would otherwise have its
refusals silently dropped, which reads as a request that was never answered);
and the gate still refuses what this client does not route, so the census cannot
be satisfied by a pattern that matches the world.

title: refactor(vtc): one place that packs a Trust Task for the wire
body:
`registry::messaging::send_didcomm` and `hooks::writer::send_envelope` were
byte-identical apart from the error type they mapped into: same envelope, same
`pack_encrypted` arguments, same `Delivery::BestEffort`, same four failure
strings. A third caller would have been a third copy.

Copies of a carriage are not merely wasteful. Each one is a place the envelope
`type` can be got wrong, and getting it wrong fails **silently** — a conformant
peer cannot distinguish "not an envelope" from "not addressed to me", so it
drops the message and answers nothing. That is the failure this workspace spent
this week chasing on the TSP side.

`crate::outbound` is now the only place either happens, and the envelope type is
not a parameter: a caller cannot pass a message type, so the mistake is
unrepresentable rather than merely avoided.

## The proof is an unused import

Removing the last packing site from each file left `Message`, `Delivery`, `Uuid`
and `TRUST_TASK_ENVELOPE_TYPE` unused in both. **Neither file names a transport
type any more** — which is a better demonstration than any assertion that there
is nothing left in them that could send. #1478 used the same proof when
`webvh_didcomm` stopped hand-rolling DIDComm.

## The TSP constant that could not drift-detect

`registry::messaging` mirrored `trust_tasks_tsp::ENVELOPE_TYPE` as a local
`const` and built the wrapper with `json!`, guarded by a test whose comment said
it was "pinned against `trust_tasks_tsp::ENVELOPE_TYPE`". It was not: it
asserted one local literal equalled another local literal, so it passed whatever
the published binding did and could never have caught the drift it described.

Both are gone. The seal is `vta_sdk::tsp_binding::wrap_envelope` — the
workspace's one implementation, whose constant comes from the binding crate, and
which writes the document bytes without reparsing them (the only step in the
path that could change what was signed). The replacement test compares the seal
against `vta_sdk::tsp_binding::ENVELOPE_TYPE`, so there is no local copy left to
disagree with.

## Scope

Packing, not transport *selection*. `vta-service`'s seam also picks a protocol by
intersecting `Protocol::PREFERENCE_ORDER` with the peer's advertisements; here
the registry client still selects and the hook writer is DIDComm by
construction. Selection belongs on top of one packer, not mixed into the change
that creates it.

`OutboundError` is three variants rather than this service's richer error types:
a caller knows whether its own failure is transient, and mapping one of these
into that is a line. Returning `RegistryError` from the seam would have made the
hook writer depend on the registry's vocabulary for no reason.

title: feat(vtc): route rooms tasks by payload type, so the served list is the router
body:
Eleven hand-written match arms, eleven copied URI entries, and a census test
whose only job was to keep the two in step — replaced by eleven registrations
that name a Rust type and nothing else.

    .on_async(handle_create)
    .on_async(handle_put_record)
    …

`trust_tasks_rs::AsyncDispatcher` derives the rest from
`Payload::TYPE_URI`: the route, the downcast, version routing, and
`unsupportedType`-vs-`unsupportedVersion`. **No URI literal appears at any
registration site**, and `registered_uris()` is the served list rather than a
second copy of it.

## The failure this makes unrepresentable

`rooms/records/curate` was dispatched by the match and named in neither URI
array, so the census passed while curate was missing from every version hint
this service emitted. Two descriptions of one fact agree right up until someone
adds to one of them.

There is now one description. `unsupported_type_or_version` reads
`served_uris()` — the routing table itself — so a hint cannot name a task nobody
serves, nor omit one that is served.

## What each piece became

- `dispatch_typed`: 64 lines of rooms arms → one guarded arm.
- `DISPATCHED_URIS`: eleven rooms entries deleted.
- `parse_payload`: gone from all eleven handlers. The dispatcher downcasts once,
  and a handler receives `TrustTask<CreateRoomBody>` rather than parsing `Value`
  and hoping.
- The four document helpers (`success_response`, `reject_with`,
  `reject_with_code`, `app_error_to_reject`) are generic over the payload. They
  only ever read the envelope; pinning them to `Value` was the thing standing
  between the handlers and their own types.
- `dispatch_or_reject` builds the framework's error document for a payload that
  does not downcast, so nothing reconstructs one — and nothing clones the
  document to keep a copy for the error path.

## The census that remains, and why

Registration cannot check that a verb was not *forgotten*: a missing
`.on_async` is silent, and the task simply is not served.
`rooms_dispatcher_serves_every_wire_uri` compares the dispatcher's own list
against `vti_rooms::wire`'s constants, which `vti-rooms/tests/
schema_conformance.rs` in turn pins against the published `TYPE_URI`s. That is a
claim worth holding; "do our two lists agree" was not.

## The tests got stronger, not weaker

The shims route through `rooms::handlers::dispatch` — the production path — so a
handler registered under the wrong type, or not registered at all, now fails in
the suite instead of in a deployment. 28 rooms tests, up from 26.

`RoomCtx` is owned rather than borrowed because `AsyncDispatcher` requires each
handler's future to be `'static`. It carries `AppState` (cheap to clone: handles,
not data) and the verified presenter — and deliberately no `JoinAuthCtx`, no ACL,
no session, so invariant I5 stays structural rather than remembered.

title: feat(process-attestation): add Process Attestation Trust Task 0.1
body:
Proposed in #8 (originally filed as #7, converted to a discussion). This is the v0.2 @stormer78 asked for, opened as a diff rather than described.

## What it adds

`specs/process-attestation/0.1/` — a Trust Task for verifying that an artifact was produced through a captured process, with evidence bound to the act of production rather than to a downstream claim about the producer. The interaction is bilateral: no registry, governing body, or third-party intermediary participates.

The task standardizes the request/response interaction and the Holder's commitment to the response. It does **not** define the receipt format, the capture primitive, or the receipt's cryptography. `assessment.determination` is deliberately not normalized across primitives, because a determination means only what the primitive that produced it defines it to mean.

## The gap it fills

The registry's ~30 domains answer three shapes of question: what credential does this party hold (`credential-exchange`, `credentials`, `vault`, `vrc`), what authority applies to this entity (`acl`, `policy`, `governance`, `registry`), and did this exchange reach its outcome (`confirm`, `task-consent`, `trust-ceremony-receipt`). None answers what process produced a given artifact.

`witness/session/submit` is the nearest neighbor and does not cover it: its evidence is that a presentation happened and a witness observed it, so the artifact under scrutiny is the presentation, not something produced beforehand. `trust-ceremony-receipt` verifies exchange-context evidence; this verifies production-context evidence. @sankarshanmukhopadhyay drew that line in #8 and I have written the spec to sit alongside it rather than overlap it.

## Decisions worth reviewer attention

**`category: framework`**, following `trust-ceremony-receipt`. TT_CATEGORIES is a closed enum and adding to it is a deliberate spec-meta-schema PR. @sankarshanmukhopadhyay suggested a distinct Process Attestation category in #8; if the WG prefers that, I will send the meta-schema PR and this becomes a one-line change. Tell me which and I will follow it.

**Response is a `oneOf` tagged on `result`**, so the attested/unavailable coupling is enforced by the generated types rather than by prose: an `Unavailable` variant cannot carry an `assessment`. Both branches share one response type, so the envelope carries no observable distinction between "no receipt held" and "declining to say" — the privacy property @sankarshanmukhopadhyay asked for when he argued against splitting the response type.

**Disclosure categories return derived aggregates only.** The primitive behind this holds raw inter-keystroke timing and a behavioral fingerprint. Returning those would be `exposure.discloses: secret`, which makes the task consequential under SPEC §2, so raw-sample disclosure is explicitly out of scope for 0.1 and noted as a future profile.

**Not `bearer`.** The response is scoped to the challenge one Verifier supplied; accepting it audience-free would expose it to cross-recipient replay (SPEC §10.1). The Security & Privacy section says why this differs from `trust-ceremony-receipt`.

**`confidence` is an integer percentage, not a fraction.** No other spec in the registry puts a floating-point value on the wire, and I found out why: a float inside an internally-tagged enum does not round-trip through the generated Rust. Worth knowing if anyone else adds a `oneOf` response.

## Also in this PR

One `.github/CODEOWNERS` line for the `process-attestation` namespace, per the procedure documented at the top of that file. Flagging it explicitly so it is not read as a request for review rights beyond this slug.

## Local verification

`npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features`, `cargo test --workspace --all-features`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, and `tsc --noEmit` all pass. Rust and TS bindings are regenerated and committed; no library version bumps or CHANGELOG entries, per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.

## Open question

`payload.invalid-examples.json` fixtures validate against the top-level request schema, so the response-side branch constraints have no negative coverage. Is there a mechanism for testing response sub-schemas that I have missed?

title: feat(vtc): verify a Trust Task's proof in the spine, where the bytes still exist
body:
feat(vtc): verify a Trust Task's proof in the spine, where the bytes still exist A proof covers the document as it was **sent**. `rooms/*` handlers verified it themselves, from the `TrustTask` they were handed — which works only while they are handed the document verbatim. They cannot keep doing that. Keying dispatch on the payload type hands a handler `TrustTask

`, and re-deriving the signed bytes from a parsed payload is sound only if `P` round-trips losslessly. None does: parse a document into a type that does not know one of its members and the member is gone, so the canonicalisation differs and a valid proof is refused. Pinned by `vta-sdk/tests/typed_proof_verify.rs`. So verification moves to `dispatch_trust_task_core`, which is the last point at which the received bytes exist, and the verified signer travels on `JoinAuthCtx`. ## Gated on the specification, so nothing existing moves The spine verifies when — and only when — `Payload::IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` says to, read through `schema_index::spec_policy_for` from the same generated bindings the schemas come from. title: feat(sdk): verify a Trust Task proof against the typed document
body:
`verify_trust_task_proof_with` took `&TrustTask`. That constrained nothing cryptographically — `eddsa-jcs-2022` canonicalises whatever serialises, and the payload's Rust shape is not part of the proof — while forcing every typed caller to convert first. The conversion is the hazard, not the cost. Re-serialising a document *before* checking its signature is the one step in the path that can change what was signed; `vta_sdk::tsp_binding::wrap_envelope` hand-rolls its JSON rather than reparse-and-reserialise for exactly this reason, on the carriage side. ## Why now Keying dispatch on the type (`trust_tasks_rs::AsyncDispatcher`, the mechanism chosen for the VTC/openvtc carriage work) hands a handler `TrustTask

`. Every proof-checking handler would then have had to round-trip back to `Value` purely to satisfy this signature — a mandatory reserialise, immediately before the signature check, in the part of the system where that is least acceptable. ## Scope `P: Serialize + Clone + Sync`. `Sync` is required by the underlying `DataIntegrityProof::verify`, which is already generic over the document; this crate was the only thing pinning the shape. Existing `&TrustTask` call sites are unaffected — `P` infers — and the whole workspace compiles unchanged, which is the check that matters for the twenty-odd callers in `vtc-service` and `vta-service`. A generalisation like this is ordinarily source-compatible, but it is a published crate's public signature and coercing the function to a concrete `fn` pointer would no longer work. Deliberately **not** marked `!`: release-plz runs `cargo-semver-checks` against the published baseline and will assign the bump from what actually changed. That check has already corrected me once this week, on a module I wrongly believed had never shipped — so the honest move is to let it read the API rather than assert the answer here. ## Tests `vta-sdk/tests/typed_proof_verify.rs` signs a document as `Value`, parses it into a typed payload exactly as a type-keyed dispatcher would, and verifies *that* — the claim being that a proof survives the downcast. The negative half edits one payload field after signing and requires a refusal, so the positive test cannot pass against a verifier that had quietly stopped checking.

title: feat(keys): ML-DSA key types and signature algorithms
body:
`keyType` gains `mldsa44` and `mldsa65`; `SignAlgorithm` gains `ML-DSA-44` and
`ML-DSA-65`. Edits in place on the existing `keys/_shared/0.1` components —
adding a permitted enumeration value to a non-discriminating field is
backwards-compatible under SPEC.md §5.2, so it relaxes a constraint rather than
narrowing one and mints no new component or specification version.

## Why two ML-DSA parameter sets

They are not redundant. W3C Quantum-Resistant Cryptosuites v1.0 defines Data
Integrity suites only for ML-DSA-44 (`mldsa44-jcs-2024`, `mldsa44-rdfc-2024`),
while Trust Spanning Protocol Rev 3 §8.1 mandates ML-DSA-65. The parameter set
is chosen by whatever consumes the key, never by the holder, so a custodian
serving both has to hold both. The descriptions say so, because the natural
instinct on seeing two adjacent parameter sets is to delete one.

## The casing differs between the two enumerations on purpose

| | values | why |
|---|---|---|
| `keyType` | `mldsa44`, `mldsa65` | specification-defined; stays lowercase beside `ed25519` / `p256` |
| `SignAlgorithm` | `ML-DSA-44`, `ML-DSA-65` | JOSE identifiers — externally owned, carried verbatim, never re-cased (§4.10 rule 5) |

The `SignAlgorithm` strings are exactly what RFC 9964 registers in the JOSE Web
Signature and Encryption Algorithms registry. Both descriptions explain the
mismatch so it does not read as a normalization defect and get "fixed".

## Growth

The generated libraries already anticipate this: `trust-tasks-codegen` marks
every generated enum `#[non_exhaustive]` precisely *"so that a value added to a
schema's `enum` is not a break either"*, following the `StandardCode` precedent
from 0.7.0. A Rust consumer absorbs these two, and the next ones, without a
compile error.

**The TypeScript side is worth a reviewer's eye.** `KeyType` is a string-literal
union, which widens rather than breaks for a consumer *reading* a value — but a
consumer with an exhaustive `switch` and a `never` check needs a new arm. That
is the same trade every enum addition here has made, and this follows #344,
which added four `Capability` values as a `feat` without `!`. Flagging it so you
can disagree rather than discover it.

Both descriptions also carry the consumer rule the framework already applies to
hash agility: a consumer that does not implement a value it receives MUST refuse
the document rather than substitute one it does support.

## Checks

Bindings regenerated (`cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen`, `npm run
build-ts-bindings`); 44 Rust test suites green under `--no-fail-fast`;
`cargo fmt --all --check` clean. No version or changelog edited.

title: feat(rooms): the wire types name the task they are the payload of
body:
Groundwork for keying dispatch on the **type** rather than on a URI written out
at the registration site. `trust_tasks_rs::Payload` is the framework's statement
that a Rust type *is* the payload of a task URI; with it, a dispatcher derives
routing, `unsupportedType`-vs-`unsupportedVersion`, and its own served-URI list
from the registrations themselves.

The URI stops being an argument someone has to supply correctly. That matters
here because this repo has already shipped the bug that a string-keyed router
invites: `rooms/records/curate` was dispatched and named in neither URI list, so
every version hint the service emitted was wrong about it. The list and the
router were two descriptions of one fact, and they disagreed.

## This does not adopt the generated types

`wire.rs`'s header argues at length for keeping these hand-written — the
generated bindings use newtypes, `NonZeroU64`, `#[non_exhaustive]` and builders,
which are right for a client constructing a request and friction for a crate
whose types are also its storage records. Nothing here reverses that.

`Payload` is a trait, not a type. Implementing it says what a type is *for* on
the wire and leaves its Rust shape exactly as the storage layer needs it. The
generated bindings stay the authority on the schema, which is what the new flags
test reads them for.

## The flags test failed on its first run, against this commit's own impls

`Payload`'s policy consts all default to `false`, so an omission is silent
**and permissive**. Writing the impls with only `TYPE_URI` gave:

    rooms/create/0.1:  left: (false, false, false, false)
                      right: (false, true,  true,  true)

Every `rooms/*` request declares `proof`, `recipient` and `issuedAt` REQUIRED in
its published schema. A missing `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` would mean unsigned requests
accepted for a task whose specification demands a proof — and no round-trip test
could see it, because both ends of the round trip are this same struct. That is
the same shape as the defect `tests/schema_conformance.rs` exists to prevent, in
a dimension that file does not cover: it checks what these types *serialise to*,
not what the framework is told to *require* of them.

So the flags are read from `schema_index::spec_policy_for` — the same published
schemas — and pinned per type. A task with no published schema yet is skipped
rather than failed, and becomes a check the moment one publishes.

## trust-tasks-rs becomes a normal dependency

It was a dev-dependency. The impls are production API, and the orphan rule
leaves no choice about where they live: `Payload` is foreign and these types are
this crate's, so the impls belong here or nowhere — a consumer cannot add them.

title: feat(vtc): accept a Trust Task in the DIDComm binding envelope
body:
This service has one dispatcher and three ways in. REST and TSP each reach it in
a single hop — TSP's inbound has no type surface at all, it opens carriage and
hands over bytes. DIDComm had a hand-written router keyed on **task URIs**, so a
verb was reachable there only if somebody had also written it down in
`messaging::route`.

**Thirteen of the twenty-four dispatched URIs had not been**: every `rooms/*`
task and both `members/personhood/*` verbs. They dispatch over REST and TSP and
answered `unsupported message type` over DIDComm — not because the service lacks
them, but because the router is a second list nobody remembered to extend. That
class of omission has already shipped here once: `rooms/records/curate` was
dispatched and named in neither URI list, so every version hint this service
emitted was wrong.

One arm fixes all thirteen, because the binding envelope's type says "a Trust
Task is inside" and nothing more. The document names the task and the spine
routes on that, so a verb is reachable because it is *dispatched* — not because
it appears in two places.

## An enveloped request was previously dropped in silence

The envelope arm in `dispatch` existed, but only as reply demux: it completed a
waiter and returned `None` **unconditionally**. So a request in the binding
envelope was accepted by the transport, matched against no waiter, and discarded
without an answer — a conformant peer built on `trust-tasks-didcomm` could not
reach this service over DIDComm at all, and saw a timeout rather than a refusal.

The waiter now decides: `complete` returns `true` only when a waiter took the
document, so a capability write reply is still absorbed and anything else falls
through to routing.

## The generic arm uses only the proven sender

`auth_sender` is the authcrypt-proven DID; the plaintext `msg.from` is never
consulted. Some per-verb handlers do consult it, deliberately, for public reads

title: feat(vtc): accept a Trust Task in the DIDComm binding envelope (#1497)
body:
feat(vtc): accept a Trust Task in the DIDComm binding envelope (#1497)

This service has one dispatcher and three ways in. REST and TSP each reach it in
a single hop — TSP's inbound has no type surface at all, it opens carriage and
hands over bytes. DIDComm had a hand-written router keyed on **task URIs**, so a
verb was reachable there only if somebody had also written it down in
`messaging::route`.

**Thirteen of the twenty-four dispatched URIs had not been**: every `rooms/*`
task and both `members/personhood/*` verbs. They dispatch over REST and TSP and
answered `unsupported message type` over DIDComm — not because the service lacks
them, but because the router is a second list nobody remembered to extend. That
class of omission has already shipped here once: `rooms/records/curate` was
dispatched and named in neither URI list, so every version hint this service
emitted was wrong.

One arm fixes all thirteen, because the binding envelope's type says "a Trust
Task is inside" and nothing more. The document names the task and the spine
routes on that, so a verb is reachable because it is *dispatched* — not because
it appears in two places.

## An enveloped request was previously dropped in silence

The envelope arm in `dispatch` existed, but only as reply demux: it completed a
waiter and returned `None` **unconditionally**. So a request in the binding
envelope was accepted by the transport, matched against no waiter, and discarded
without an answer — a conformant peer built on `trust-tasks-didcomm` could not
reach this service over DIDComm at all, and saw a timeout rather than a refusal.

The waiter now decides: `complete` returns `true` only when a waiter took the
document, so a capability write reply is still absorbed and anything else falls
through to routing.

## The generic arm uses only the proven sender

`auth_sender` is the authcrypt-proven DID; the plaintext `msg.from` is never
consulted. Some per-verb handlers do consult it, deliberately, for public reads
— but a generic arm cannot make that judgement per task, and defaulting to the

title: fix(didcomm): route the binding envelopes, which we already send
body:
`OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` decides whether an inbound message reaches
`process_inbound_message` at all — anything it does not list is dropped at
`didcomm.rs:1188` with a `debug!` and no reply. It listed task URIs only, and a
binding envelope deliberately names no task, so it listed none of them.

That was a hole in both directions at once:

- `capabilities::send_capability_document` sends with
  `TRUST_TASK_ENVELOPE_TYPE`, and the VTC's hook relay answers in kind.
- `message_dispatch::process_inbound_message:279` has a branch for exactly that
  type.
- Every such reply was dropped *between* them.

A handler that exists and is unreachable looks precisely like a peer that never
answered, which is why this survived: nothing is red, and the symptom is a
capability write that appears to go unacknowledged.

The arm is `https://trusttasks\.org/binding/.*` rather than the one DIDComm
constant, so the TSP envelope is covered by the same rule — this crate already
opens that one inbound (`tsp_document_to_message`) and sends it (#327), and a
gate that admitted one carriage but not the other would be a third dialect
rather than a fix.

Two tests: one pins both envelope URIs, and one asserts the constant this crate
*sends* with is routed, read from `capabilities::TRUST_TASK_ENVELOPE_TYPE`
rather than retyped — so the gate cannot drift from what actually goes on the
wire, which is how the hole opened in the first place.

Additive: nothing changes what this crate sends, and every existing arm stays.

title: ci(release): restore the vti-secrets semver check, now its baseline builds
body:
#1492 switched this check off because the baseline could not be compiled at all:
`vti-secrets 0.3.7` predated the `aws-smithy-types >=1.6.1, <1.7` bound, so
building its rustdoc resolved 1.7.0 and `aws-smithy-json 0.63` failed against
it. The entry was written to be deleted after the first release that published
the crate, and that release has happened.

`vti-secrets 0.3.8` is on crates.io and its manifest carries the bound:

    aws-smithy-types: req=">=1.6.1, <1.7"

Verified rather than assumed — against a **cold** `cargo-semver-checks` cache,
because a warm one reuses baseline rustdoc built before 1.7.0 existed and hides
exactly this:

    cargo semver-checks --package vti-secrets --baseline-version 0.3.8
    Summary no semver update required
    Finished [ 126.441s] vti-secrets

So the deadlock is gone — the check that was impossible is merely a check again,
and the crate goes back to being covered like the other seven with external
consumers.

title: fix(tsp): carry Trust Tasks in the binding envelope, both directions
body:
This crate spoke its own TSP dialect: it sealed the **bare** Trust Task document
where the published binding
(`https://trusttasks.org/binding/tsp/0.1/envelope`) wraps it as
`{"type", "document"}`. It reached the VTC only because that service accepts
both shapes. A conformant peer refuses it, and the VTA does:

    refused a TSP frame that is not a binding envelope
      reason=TSP payload is not a `…/binding/tsp/0.1/envelope` envelope
             (got `…/spec/keys/export-secret/0.1`)

which the sender experiences as a reply that never comes. VTI #1488 moved every
client in that workspace onto the binding; this is the same change here, using
the same function rather than a fourth local spelling of the same JSON.

## The receive half, which is the part that would have bitten

`tsp_document_to_message` read `doc["type"]` straight off the payload. An
envelope has a `type` of its own — the binding's — so wrapping the send without
touching this would have routed every reply to a handler that does not exist:
the send succeeds, the peer answers, the answer evaporates on arrival. Silent,
like the rest of this class.

It now opens the envelope first, and still accepts a bare document: this is a
client reading whatever a community sends it, and a VTC predating the binding
sends bare. The two shapes are unambiguous, so being liberal costs nothing,
while being strict would turn "an older peer" into a silent drop — the failure
being fixed, not a stricter version of it.

Three tests pin it: an enveloped frame yields the **task** type rather than the
binding's, a bare one still maps, and both produce an identical message.

## vta-sdk 0.38.2

Picked up for `vta_sdk::tsp_binding`, which is where VTI put the one
implementation of this binding (`vta-service` uses the same function). The
update also unifies `trust-tasks-rs` at 0.20.6 — `cargo tree -d` shows no second
copy of it, `vta-sdk`, or any wire crate.

## Not in this change

DIDComm carriage here still types a message with the **task** URI
(`Message::build(id, JOIN_REQUEST_SUBMIT_TYPE, body)`) where the binding says
`trust_tasks_didcomm::ENVELOPE_TYPE` with the task inside. That works only
because `vtc-service` dispatches on task URIs — the same private-dialect shape
this commit removes from TSP. It is a wire change across two repos and needs the
VTC accepting both types before this side flips, so it belongs in its own
sequenced pair rather than smuggled in here.

title: vti-secrets-v0.3.8
body:
### Fixed

- **deps**: Bound aws-smithy-types below 1.7, which breaks aws-smithy-json 0.63 ([#1485](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1485))

A fresh dependency resolution stopped compiling:

      error[E0308]: expected `DocumentObject`, found `HashMap<String, Document>`
        --> aws-smithy-json-0.63.0/src/codec/deserializer.rs:707:37
      error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&_` not covered
        --> aws-smithy-json-0.63.0/src/serialize.rs:36:15

  `aws-smithy-types` 1.7.0 changed `Document::Object` from
  `HashMap<String, Document>` to a new `DocumentObject`, and added a variant
  to an enum that is `#[non_exhaustive]` — a breaking change shipped as a
  MINOR bump. `aws-smithy-json` 0.63.0 declares `aws-smithy-types = "^1.6.1"`,
  which admits 1.7.0 and then does not compile against it.

  Cargo unifies `aws-smithy-types` to one version across the graph but keeps
  both `aws-smithy-json` 0.63 and 0.64 — 0.x minors are incompatible majors —
  so the two coexist and only the 0.63 copy breaks. We have both because
  `aws-sdk-secretsmanager` 1.116.0 moved to json `^0.64.0` while `aws-config`
  1.12.0, its newest release, still wants `^0.63.0`. Both reach us:
  `vti-secrets` behind `aws-secrets`, and `vta-tee` unconditionally, so a
  plain `cargo build --workspace` is affected as well as the secrets path.

  Cargo.lock already held 1.6.3, so committed builds were never affected and
  only a lockless resolution broke — which is what `cargo install --path`
  does unless given `--locked`. That is how this was met:

      cargo install --path vtc-service --no-default-features \
        --features setup,website,admin-ui,aws-secrets,tsp

  `--locked` remains the right flag for a reproducible install. This bound is
  what keeps `cargo update` and a lockless build honest too.

  The bound is declared once in `[workspace.dependencies]` with the
  reasoning, and referenced from the two crates that pull `aws-config` —
  Cargo only honours a version requirement from a crate that declares it, so
  a workspace entry alone would constrain nothing. Neither crate calls it.

  `>= 1.6.1, < 1.7` rather than `= 1.6.3`: 1.6.1 is aws-smithy-json 0.63.0's
  own floor, and the upper bound excludes the break without freezing out
  patch releases in the working line. **Remove it when `aws-config` ships a
  release on json 0.64.**

  Verified, on this branch:

    - without the bound, a lockless resolve picks aws-smithy-types 1.7.0 with
      aws-smithy-json 0.63.0 AND 0.64.0 — the failing combination
    - with it, a lockless resolve picks 1.6.3, json 0.63.0 alone, and backs
      aws-sdk-secretsmanager off to 1.115.0
    - Cargo.lock moves by two lines, both dependency edges; no version churn
    - `cargo check -p vti-secrets --no-default-features --features aws-secrets`
      and `cargo check -p vtc-service --no-default-features --features
      setup,website,admin-ui,aws-secrets,tsp` both pass
