title: feat(did-webvh): honour addTspService on a template-rendered DID (#1424)
body:
feat(did-webvh): honour addTspService on a template-rendered DID (#1424)

`vta/webvh/dids/create` accepts `addTspService`, and for every DID minted from a
template it was silently dropped. A rendered template is treated as a
caller-supplied document, so it never reaches the builder `with_tsp_service`
(#959) feeds — the flag went into `additional_services`, and nothing read them.
A room, a room host, or any other templated identity could not advertise TSP
however it was asked, and the response gave no sign.

Found from the console side: its New room form could not offer TSP on a room or
its host, and asking the agent to add it did nothing.

`with_tsp_in_rendered_document` applies the flag to the rendered document
itself, right after render, using `vta_sdk::did_templates::tsp_service` so the
entry is the same shape `vtc-host` and `didcomm-mediator` publish, and ending
with the same canonical sort (TSP > DIDComm > REST) every other transport path
uses.

## Two deliberate differences from `with_tsp_service`

- **The endpoint is the document's mediator, not this VTA's.** A template names
  its own (`MEDIATOR_DID`), and TSP binds the same mediator DIDComm does (D8,
  §14 Q2). Advertising this VTA's mediator on a document routed elsewhere would
  give one DID a different mediator per protocol. The mediator is read off the
  document's `DIDCommMessaging` entry in any of the three `serviceEndpoint`
  shapes, and only a DID counts.
- **`services.tsp` is not consulted.** That gate stops this VTA claiming a
  transport *its own stack* cannot carry, on documents routed to its own
  mediator. A templated DID's holder is usually something else — room-host
  serving at its own `--mediator-did` (#1418), a community — and whether that
  holder decodes TSP is the caller's claim, exactly as `SERVICE_TSP` is at
  provisioning.

## Refused, not skipped

A document that names no DIDComm mediator cannot carry a TSP entry — there is no
mediator to name — so the request is refused with a validation error rather than
minting without the entry the caller asked for, which is the defect this
replaces. A document that already carries `TSPTransport` (`ai-agent`, the
`did-host-*tsp` templates) keeps it and gains no second one.

Not asked, a rendered document is exactly what its template produced.

## Tests

Rendered from the real built-ins the way `create_did_webvh` renders them, so a
template that changes its service block fails here rather than at a mint: `room`
gains TSP at its own mediator; `room-host` keeps `VTARest` in canonical order;
the flag off leaves the document byte-identical; `ai-agent` is not given a second
`#tsp`; `did-host-http` (no mediator) is refused; and the mediator is found in
every `serviceEndpoint` shape while a URL is not.

## What this does not change

Nothing answers as a room's DID today — the VTA's mediator sessions are all
opened as its own DID — so TSP on a room DID is an advertisement, as the room's
existing DIDComm entry already is. On a room host started with `--mediator-did`
it is served. The console says which.

The plugin sends `addTspService` from its New room form in
OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin (companion PR); the two cut over together.

title: feat(audit): verify the VTA's audit chain
body:
Stacked on #1420. Chaining that nobody can check is a hash column rather than tamper-evidence, so this is the half that makes the chain testable.

Reads the audit keyspace in **write order** — the chain is a strict left fold, and verifying it in any other order reports breaks that are not there — and returns a report.

## The report separates two counts that look alike

A row that is not a chainable envelope means opposite things depending on where it sits:

- **before the chain opened** — expected. The VTA audited to this keyspace before its log was chained, and nothing committed to those rows at the time. Counted as `preChainRows`, not faulted.
- **after the chain opened** — a **finding**. Everything the sink writes from that point is an envelope, so a row that is not one arrived by another route. That is what an insertion looks like.

A third count, `legacyEnvelopesSkipped`, is a finding wherever the chain has opened: the verifier passes over those rather than checking them, so **an envelope forged with an older schema version passes untouched**. The VTC's equivalent already records this; it matters more here because a VTA legitimately has pre-chain history and the two are easy to conflate.

The shape follows the VTC's `VerifyResponse` rather than inventing one, with the pre-chain distinction added because only a VTA has that history.

## Tests

- a pre-chain row is counted and not faulted;
- the same row after the chain opened is reported as a finding;
- a tampered entry — an outcome rewritten in place, hashes left alone, the edit someone covering their tracks would make — is caught and reported with **where** it broke;
- and in the sink, that 25 writes inside one second still verify, which is the property the storage key's nanosecond field exists for.

One of these caught a bug in its own fixture: the seeded "pre-chain" key was 17 digits rather than the 20 the format uses, so it sorted *after* the chained rows and was counted as an insertion. The test failed for exactly the right reason.

## Still open

The surface: a Trust Task and a `pnm audit verify` subcommand, matching the VTC's `/v1/audit/verify` and `cnm audit verify`. And retention versus the chain, which the design note covers.

title: feat(audit): verify the VTA's audit chain (#1421)
body:
feat(audit): verify the VTA's audit chain (#1421)

* feat(audit): verify the VTA's audit chain

Chaining that nobody can check is a hash column, not tamper-evidence.
This reads the audit keyspace in write order and reports what it found,
including the parts a bare verified/not-verified answer hides.

The report separates two counts that look alike and mean opposite
things. A row that is not a chainable envelope is expected before the
chain opened — the VTA audited to this keyspace before its log was
chained, and nothing committed to those rows at the time. The same row
after the chain opened is a finding: everything the sink writes from
that point is an envelope, so a row that is not one arrived by another
route, which is what an insertion looks like. Envelopes the verifier
passes over by schema version are counted separately again, because a
forged old-schema envelope passes untouched and a reader who sees only
verified: true has been told less than they think.

Tests cover both readings of an unchained row, a tampered entry
reported with where it broke, and — in the sink — that writes inside
one second still verify, which is the property the storage key's
nanoseconds exist for.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(audit): expose chain verification as a task and a command (#1422)

The verifier had no caller. This adds the task, the client method and
pnm audit verify, so an operator can ask the question and a monitor can
ask it on a schedule.

Admin only, and for the same reason reading the log is: whether the
record of what everyone did is intact is itself a privileged question.

The command prints the counts whether or not they are zero, because
zero is the interesting answer and an operator who has to remember to
ask has not been told. Where a count is non-zero it says what the
number means — rows written after the chain opened that are not chained
arrived by another route, and envelopes skipped by schema version were
passed over rather than checked, so a forged one passes here untouched.

It exits non-zero on any finding, not only on a broken chain. A report
that says verified: true beside a count of unchained rows and still
exits zero is one nobody wires an alert to.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(audit): bind verify on the authority this project controls

The manifest test refused the new URI, and it was right to: it was
bound under spec/vta/, the authority the canonical registry serves,
and nothing there publishes a schema for it. A URI on that authority is
a claim that the registry has specified the operation, so binding one
before the spec exists asserts something untrue — which is why the test
says that raising its count is the wrong fix.

Moved to openvtc/vta/audit/verify/1.0, beside the VTC's own
openvtc/vtc/audit/verify/1.0. It moves to spec/ if and when the
operation is specified upstream, which is the route every other family
here has taken.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(audit): keep the chain verifiable across a retention sweep (#1423)

* feat(audit): keep the chain verifiable across a retention sweep

Retention deletes the oldest entries, so the oldest survivor points
back at something that is gone — which is exactly what an entry removed
by an attacker looks like. Retention and tamper-evidence were therefore
mutually exclusive: the first person to run verify after a sweep would
have got a failure that means nothing.

The sweep now leaves a watermark: the hash it pruned through and how
many chained entries it removed. Verification resumes from there rather
than expecting a chain back to the opening, and reports that it did,
along with how many entries it could not check.

The report says so because the claim is weaker than it looks. The
pruned entries were not verified and cannot be — they are gone. What
holds is that the survivors continue a chain that ran through the
watermark, and the watermark lives in the same store as the log, so an
adversary who can delete entries can rewrite it to match. It restores
verification across an honest sweep, which is what retention needs, and
nothing more. Signing it and publishing it outside the store is the
stronger answer, and is what the VTC's checkpoints do.

The sweep gains a cutoff-taking form so the boundary can be tested:
derived from the clock, the only boundaries reachable in a test are a
whole day ago and nothing. A test found the watermark path this way,
and a second test pins that a removal after the sweep still breaks the
chain — the watermark must not become a way to hide one.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* style(audit): collapse the nested let-chain in the sweep

Clippy's collapsible-if, and CI denies warnings.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(mcp): classify tasks bound on the authority we control

The guard derives a task's risk from its slug, and read the slug only
from the canonical authority. A task bound on openvtc/vta — which is
where an operation lives until it is specified upstream — produced no
slug at all, so it fell through to the mutating default and the census
test refused it as unclassified.

Both prefixes now yield the same slug. That keeps an operator's pattern
matching across the move from one authority to the other, and it stops
a task escaping classification by being bound on exactly the authority
it is supposed to be bound on while it waits for a spec.

The verify verb joins the read list: checking the audit log's hash
chain reads the whole log and writes nothing, and the answer being
'broken' is a fact about what is already there.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* revert(audit): unbind verify until its spec is published upstream

Three census tests refused the binding, from three directions, and
together they say one thing: a new VTA Trust Task needs its spec
published upstream first.

The canonical authority refuses a URI the registry does not serve. The
authority this project controls is not available to a VTA task at all —
the SDK requires every catalogued URI to be canonical, and the
framework's parser rejects the other shape. And the per-URI list of
things bound ahead of their spec says in terms not to grow it.

That is the rule this workspace has, and it is the rule the VTI
specification states: a canonical name requires a published
specification of the thing named. Both of my attempts were attempts to
route around it.

So the operation stays and the surface waits. verify_audit_chain, the
report, the retention watermark and their tests are untouched — what is
removed is the task URI, its handler and dispatch entry, the client
method and pnm audit verify. They come back when the spec lands
upstream, against the canonical URI, which is where they should have
been bound from the start.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(audit): bind verify to the canonical task that already specifies it

The operation did not need a new URI. audit/verify/0.1 is specified in
the canonical catalogue and served by the registry this workspace
already pins — I invented spec/vta/audit/verify/1.0 without checking,
and the three census tests that refused it were each pointing at that.

Bound to the canonical URI, so the task is validated against a
published schema on every request rather than being one more thing
bound ahead of its spec.

The response follows the published shape, which cost two corrections.
head is a multibase-encoded multihash, not hex: the algorithm travels
in the value so a verifier never infers it, and the schema refuses a
bare hex string for that reason. And the canonical shape has one bucket
for rows that would not parse, where a VTA has two kinds — rows written
before its log was chained, which are expected and no chain could
cover, and rows appearing after it was, which is what an insertion
looks like. Collapsing them would report an ordinary history as a
finding or hide a finding in an ordinary history, so the total goes in
the canonical member and the breakdown in ext, under a key naming this
implementation. That is what the extension slot is for; a member beside
it would be invisible to a peer that does not know it and
indistinguishable from a typo to one that validates.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(audit): give verify its conformance witness, and name its keyspaces

Binding to a published URI is what asked for both of these, and both
are the point of binding there.

The conformance sweep requires a witness for every dispatched URI the
registry publishes: a request and a response built from the generated
wire types and round-tripped through them. audit/verify now has one,
and writing it is where a shape error would have surfaced — the head is
a multibase-encoded multihash because the schema refuses a bare hex
digest, and the witness carries a populated extension slot because this
maintainer populates it on every response, so a witness that omitted it
would not exercise the shape actually sent.

The test helper reached for its keyspaces by string literal, which the
workspace refuses: a literal is a name nobody renames with the const.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(mock): give the webvh family test a real stack

Second occurrence of a failure already recorded here: this body boots
an in-process VTA and drives a whole family through it, so the future
is enormous in a debug build and grows every time the dispatch table
does. Adding an audit/verify arm pushed it past libtest's 2 MiB.

That is not a fact about the arm. It is this test sitting just under a
limit nobody had written down — the same sentence the note on
services_write_paths_against_a_hosted_vta_did already carries, about
the same file, from when two rooms/keys arms did it.

Same fix: ask for the stack here rather than leaving it to
RUST_MIN_STACK, because a test that passes only when an environment
variable is set is a test that fails for the next person.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

feat(rooms): let each minted DID advertise TSP at its mediator

The New room form mints two DIDs — the host's and the room's — and neither could
advertise TSP. The templates publish their mediator for DIDComm only, and the
agent dropped `addTspService` for every template-rendered DID, so there was
nothing the form could have sent. The agent side is fixed in

decodes gives clients a route they will choose and cannot use — the agent takes

- **Host:** room-host started with `--mediator-did` answers TSP there as well as

title: feat(rooms): one context for a host and its rooms, and a host you finish setting up
body:
Registering a room failed against a live deployment. Following it through found a defect in what the New room form had been minting, a flow that let a room be registered with a host nobody had started, and two statements on screen that were not true. It also adds the context-first flow.

## The defect: every room minted here became its context's DID

`vta/webvh/dids/create` defaults `setPrimary` to **true** and overwrites the context's DID unconditionally (vta-service: `set_primary: body.set_primary.unwrap_or(true)`). Core's `webvhDidCreate` never sent the member, so each room minted from this form replaced its context's identity.

A room-host enrolled into a context serves **as that context's DID** — it fetches the DID's keys via `vta/contexts/secrets` at startup — so a host and a room sharing a context left the host coming up as the room.

- **Core:** `WebvhDidCreateParams.setPrimary`, forwarded whenever given (`false` included), documented as "absent is not no".
- **Form:** sends `true` for a host, `false` for every room.

> **Existing deployments:** a context that had a room minted in it from #228/#229 now acts as that room. Repair it in step 2 with **Make another of its DIDs the host** (sets the context's DID back via `vta/contexts/update-did`). The form warns about this wherever it offers a context's current DID as the host.

## One context, two kinds of DID

1. **Choose the context** — its DIDs and keys are loaded for the steps below.
2. **Set up the host** — the context's own DID:
   - use the DID it has;
   - make another of its DIDs the context's (one explicit write);
   - mint one as the context's DID (`setPrimary: true`, warns if it replaces one);
   - or paste a host run outside this agent.
3. **The room's identity** — a DID beside the host's (`setPrimary: false`), or picked from the context's DIDs with its signing key offered from the agent's key records (`{did}#…`, key-agreement keys excluded, preselected only when exactly one matches). The host's DID is never offered as a room, and a pasted one is refused.
4. **Visibility.**

Each step opens only once the previous one is ready.

**Sharing the context does not expose room keys to the host:** its grant is `application`; key export needs admin; `contexts/secrets` releases only the context DID's keys; `keys/sign` at `application` signs under `SigningDomain::Opaque`, which verifies only as an opaque-signing payload, not as a proof on a room credential. (Read from `keys.rs` and `SigningDomain`; the per-key checks inside `sign_payload` were not traced.)

## A new host is a step you finish

After minting a host DID, steps 3–4 stay closed until the operator confirms the host is running. The panel prints:

1. the certificate the hostname needs, with the one covering wildcard — `rooms.vdr.openvtc.net` needs `*.vdr.openvtc.net`, which `*.openvtc.net` does not provide (the failure that started this);
2. the `room-host` command: `--vta-did` this agent, `--vta-context` this context, `--resolve-dids`, `--mediator-did` when set;
3. the grant for the throwaway `did:key` it prints: `--role application --contexts <this context>`;
4. restart, after which it serves as the context's DID.

The confirmation is labelled as the operator's word, not a check. Commands are built in `src/manager/room-host-setup.ts` with tests: a grant without `--contexts` reaches every context, and a host without `--vta-context` enrols into `rooms` and serves as whatever DID that carries.

## Corrections to earlier copy

- **#229 said the host "does not listen" at its mediator.** That was checked against a stale VTI checkout; room-host on main (#1418) serves DIDComm and TSP at `--mediator-did`. Still true: the agent calls hosts over REST only (`OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED = [Rest]`), so the URL stays required. The copy now says the URL is for the agent and the mediator for members.
- **No TSP on a minted host DID.** The `room-host` template advertises the mediator for DIDComm only, and the agent does not apply `addTspService` to a template-rendered document. Stated in the panel as a template gap.

## Not in this PR (verifiable-trust-infrastructure)

- `rooms/owner/register` surfaces an unreachable host as the redacted internal error ("the consumer could not complete this task"). A stable code carrying the host DID and endpoint would let the console say what failed.
- The `room-host` / `room` templates publish no `TSPTransport`, and `addTspService` is ignored on the template path.

## Tests

- `packages/core/tests/webvh.dids-servers-names.mjs`: `setPrimary` false/true sent, absent omitted.
- `tests/room-host-setup.test.mts` (new): agent and context named, `--resolve-dids`, mediator present/absent, grant is application on exactly the context, shell quoting, hostname and covering wildcard.
- `tests/rooms-create.render.test.mts` (rewritten): screen order vs wire order; rooms minted `setPrimary: false`, hosts `true`; context DID offered with the check; making another DID the host is one `update-did` write; pasted outside host; mint default for a context with no DID; replacement warning; later steps locked until the host is confirmed; setup commands and certificate guidance; existing room picked from the context with its single signing key filled, several keys not preselected, host DID refused as a room, unreadable listings fall back to typing; the mediator, path and refusal cases carried over.

Checks:

- `npm test` (core): 598 pass
- `npm test` (extension): 585 pass
- `tsc -b` clean; `vite build -c vite.config.manager.ts` builds
- Checked in a Chrome tab against a stubbed agent: a context whose DID is a room (warning shown), the repair path with steps 3–4 locked, and the new-host setup panel with command, grant and certificate guidance

That matters because a room-host enrolled into a context serves as the context's
DID — it fetches that DID's keys through `vta/contexts/secrets` at startup — so a
host and a room in one context left the host coming up *as the room*. Nothing on
screen or on the wire looked wrong when it happened.

Core now carries `setPrimary`, sent whenever it is given, `false` included. The
form sends `true` for a host and `false` for every room.

## One context, two kinds of DID in it

The form asks for the context first, and a host and its rooms live in it:

1. **The context.** Its DIDs and keys are listed for the steps below.
2. **The host — the context's own DID.** Use the one it has; make another of its
   DIDs the context's (`vta/contexts/update-did`, which is also the repair for a
   context a room took over); mint one as the context's DID; or name a host run
   outside this agent.
3. **The room — a DID beside it.** Minted with `setPrimary: false`, or picked
   from the context's DIDs with its signing key offered from the agent's key
   records (`{did}#…`, the key-agreement key excluded, preselected only when
   exactly one matches). The host's DID is never offered as a room.
4. **Visibility.**

Sharing the context does not hand the host a room's keys: its grant is
`application`, exporting a key needs admin, `contexts/secrets` releases only the
context DID's keys, and `keys/sign` at `application` signs under the opaque
domain, which verifies as nothing but an opaque-signing payload.

## A new host is a step you finish

Minting a host's DID is not having a host, and registration was the first thing
to notice — as an opaque internal error from the agent. After minting, the form
prints what to do, and holds steps 3 and 4 closed until the operator confirms the
host is running:

- the certificate the host's hostname needs, naming the one wildcard that covers
  it (`*.vdr.openvtc.net` for `rooms.vdr.openvtc.net`, which a `*.openvtc.net`
  certificate does not — the failure that started this);
- the `room-host` command, with `--vta-did` this agent, `--vta-context` this
  context, `--resolve-dids`, and `--mediator-did` where there is one;
- the grant for the throwaway DID it prints: `application`, `--contexts` this
  context, never wider;
- restart, after which it serves as the context's DID.

The confirmation is labelled as the operator's word, not a check. The commands
live in `room-host-setup.ts` with their own tests, because a printed grant with
no `--contexts` reaches every context, and a host started without
`--vta-context` enrols into `rooms` and serves as whatever DID that carries.

Every later step now opens only once the one before it is ready.

## Two things the form said that were not true

- #229 said the host "does not listen" on its mediator. It was written against a
  stale checkout: room-host on main (#1418) serves DIDComm and TSP at
  `--mediator-did`. What stays true is that the agent calls hosts over REST only
  (`OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED`), so the URL is still required — the copy now says the
  URL is for the agent and the mediator for members.
- The `room-host` template advertises its mediator for DIDComm only, and the
  agent does not apply `addTspService` to a template-rendered document, so a
  minted host DID publishes no TSP entry. Said in the panel; it is a template
  gap, not a choice this form can make.

The form's shared parts moved to `rooms-create-parts.tsx`, so `rooms-create.tsx`
is about the flow.

title: feat(rooms): ask for the host first, and let a DID's path be named
body:
Follow-up to #228: the host step moves first, a DID's path can be named, and the form stops describing the host's mediator as a way in.

## What changes

### The host comes first

Step 1 is the host, step 2 the room's own identity, step 3 what the host can see. A host may have to be created before there is anywhere to put a room, so asking for it first matches the order the work happens in.

**Only the screen order moved.** The room's DID is still minted before any host is told about it (`dids/create` then `rooms/owner/register`). Both orders have their own test, since a change to one is what could quietly shift the other.

Seeding reverses: minting a host seeds the room's context, server and mediator — never over a mediator the operator picked for the room themselves.

### A DID's path can be named

Both mints offer:

- **Let the hosting server choose** — the default; `pathMode` is omitted, which is `autoAssign`.
- **Choose a name** — sent as `pathMode: { mode: "explicit", path }`, previewed as it reads in the DID (`rooms/northwind` → `…:<domain>:rooms:northwind`).

A name is checked before the mint against the hosting server's rule, mirrored in `src/manager/webvh-path.ts` from `validate_custom_path` (affinidi-webvh-service, `did-hosting-common/src/server/mnemonic.rs`): segments of 2–63 `[a-z0-9-]`, alphanumeric at both ends, `/` between them, at most 255 total, and a first segment that is not one of the server's reserved routes. Checking first is worth the copy because a refused mint can leave derived keys behind. The server stays the authority, and the module says divergence is fixed on this side.

Nothing checks that a name is **free** before minting — no task exposes that — so a taken path comes back as the mint's own error.

### The host needs a URL, and the form now says so

The host mediator's hint read "how a member with no reachable URL gets to the host". That was wrong (it came in with #226):

- the `room-host` service serves HTTP only — no mediator, DIDComm or TSP inbound;
- vta-service initiates REST only to a host (`OUTBOUND_SUPPORTED` in `vta-service/src/operations/room_host.rs`) and refuses a host without a REST endpoint as "no transport in common".

The template publishes a mediator, but nothing listens on it. The host step now says the URL carries everything today and the mediator is published but not yet answered. The URL can become optional once vta-service can initiate DIDComm/TSP and room-host listens on one.

The panel description also claimed nothing is written until Create room, which "Mint host DID" contradicts; corrected.

## Tests

- `tests/webvh-path.test.mts` (new, 10): accepted names, segment and total lengths, case/charset, edge characters, empty segments, the colon message, reserved names only as the first segment, the reserved list itself, and the DID rendering.
- `tests/rooms-create.render.test.mts`: screen order and wire order pinned separately; path absent by default, explicit when named, refused names hold the button, flipping back sends nothing; host path named; room seeded from a minted host without overwriting a chosen mediator; the URL wording, with the old mediator phrase held off screen.

Checks:

- `npm test` (extension): 569 pass, 0 fail
- `tsc -b` clean; `vite build -c vite.config.manager.ts` builds
- Checked in a Chrome tab against a stubbed agent: host step first, path preview, and a refused name's message render as intended

title: feat(rooms): walk the New room form as three explained steps
body:
The New room form was one wrap of fields under a paragraph, and the two things an operator most needed were the two that got missed: which mediator to name, and that a host DID can be minted here at all. #226's "Mint one" sat beside the HOST DID field as a quiet button and read as a label.

## What changes

The form is now **three numbered steps**, each saying what it decides and why before it asks:

1. **Give the room its own identity** — mint a new one, or use one already minted (DID + signing key ID).
2. **Choose a host for its records** — *use a host that already has a DID* or *mint a DID for a new host*, as two cards side by side. Minting opens a panel explaining what it does and does not do; afterwards a note says what still happens outside the form (the host enrols; you grant it the application role) and that registration fails until the host is up, with the identity kept for a retry.
3. **Decide how much the host can see** — private / attributed / open as cards with a sentence each, plus optional retention.

Above the button, a short list says what pressing it will do: mint the DID in the chosen context and server (the step that cannot be taken back), then register with the host. The hint beside the button names the step a missing field belongs to.

### The mediator is offered, not typed

`vta/services/list` names the mediator the agent's DIDComm and TSP transports route through, so it is shown as a card and preselected, with *a different mediator* one click away.

- DIDComm and TSP sharing one mediator is one card, not two identical choices.
- A mediator whose transport is switched off is listed but not preselected.
- The listing is admin-gated. A caller refused it is told so — a failure to ask, not an agent without a mediator — and falls back to the typed field.
- The host's mediator seeds from the room's choice.
- Worded as what the agent *routes through*, never as what works: advertisement is not availability.

### Also

- A retention that is not a whole number of days now holds the button. It used to send `Number("two weeks")`, i.e. `NaN`.
- A step is ticked only once every step above it is — step three is valid on arrival and was otherwise ticked on load.
- `services/list` reaches only `manager.js`, so the admin-surface guard's single exception still holds.

## Tests

`rooms-create.render.test.mts` now finds fields by accessible name rather than position, since fields appear and disappear with the choices above them. Eight new tests: the agent's mediator offered and chosen, a different one sent, an unreadable listing, a switched-off mediator not preselected, host minting offered before anything is pressed, the host's mediator following the room's, retention refused, and the tick order. `rooms-pane.render.test.mts` answers the new `services/list` read.

- `npm test` (extension): 550 pass, 0 fail
- `tsc -b` clean; `vite build -c vite.config.manager.ts` builds
- Checked in a Chrome tab against a stubbed agent: steps, mediator cards, host-mint panel, summary and hint all render as intended

title: feat(audit): keep the chain verifiable across a retention sweep
body:
Stacked on #1421. The last item in the audit-chaining note, and the one with a deadline attached: it only bites after the retention period has elapsed once.

## The problem

Retention deletes the oldest entries. The oldest survivor then points back at something that is gone — **which is exactly what an entry removed by an attacker looks like**. So retention and tamper-evidence were mutually exclusive, and the first person to run `pnm audit verify` after a sweep would have got a failure that means nothing.

## The fix

The sweep leaves a **watermark**: the hash it pruned through, and how many chained entries it removed. Verification resumes from there rather than expecting a chain back to the opening — `ChainVerifier::resume` already existed for exactly this.

The watermark is stored outside the `log:` prefix, because the sweep deletes by that prefix and would otherwise prune the watermark it just wrote.

## What the report now says, and why

`resumedFromPrune` and `prunedEntries`, surfaced in `pnm audit verify`, because **the claim is weaker than "verified" looks**:

> The pruned entries were not verified by this run and cannot be — they are gone. What holds is that the survivors continue a chain that ran through the watermark.

And the watermark lives in the same store as the log, so an adversary who can delete entries can rewrite it to match. **It restores verification across an honest sweep, which is what retention needs, and nothing more.** Signing it and publishing it outside the store is the stronger answer, and is what the VTC's checkpoints do — worth doing, and a separate change.

## A testability seam

`cleanup_logs_before(ks, cutoff)` beside `cleanup_expired_logs(ks, days)`. Derived from the clock, the only boundaries reachable in a test are "a whole day ago" — which nothing in a test is — and "nothing". The first version of the test asserted a sweep had pruned something and failed, correctly: at zero days' retention it had pruned nothing, because entries written this second are not older than now.

## Tests

- a pruned log still verifies, resumes from the watermark, and reports the count;
- **a removal after the sweep is still caught** — the watermark must not become a way to hide one.

title: feat(audit): expose chain verification as a task and a command
body:
Stacked on #1421, which added the verifier. This gives it callers.

- `spec/vta/audit/verify/1.0` — the task, in the namespace the VTA's own tasks already use (`spec/vta/audit/get-retention/1.0` sits beside it), registered in the dispatch table and classified `ReadOnly` for retry.
- `VtaClient::verify_audit_chain` — the client method.
- `pnm audit verify` — the command.

The report type moves to `vta-sdk::protocols::audit_management::verify` so a caller can read the answer.

**Admin only**, for the same reason reading the log is: whether the record of what everyone did is intact is itself a privileged question, and a caller who cannot read the log has no business learning whether it has been altered.

## Two choices in the command worth flagging

**It prints the counts whether or not they are zero.** Zero is the interesting answer for `preChainRows`, and an operator who has to remember to ask has not been told. Where a count is non-zero it explains what the number means rather than leaving a bare integer: rows written after the chain opened that are not chained arrived by another route; envelopes skipped by schema version were passed over rather than checked, so a forged one passes here untouched.

**It exits non-zero on any finding, not only on a broken chain.** A report that says `verified: true` beside a count of unchained rows and still exits zero is one nobody wires an alert to — and the unchained rows are exactly the case a chain alone cannot catch.

## Next

Retention versus the chain, which is the last item in the design note: a sweep deletes the tail and leaves the remainder unverifiable, indistinguishable from tampering. The VTC's checkpoint mechanism is the answer, and this command is what will show it working.

title: feat(audit): write the VTA's audit log as a hash chain
body:
Stacked on #1419. This is the piece that actually closes **VTI-AUD-004** and **VTI-AUD-005** for the VTA — the sink and the read path, which had to land together.

## What changes

The sink writes envelopes through the shared writer rather than flat rows. Each entry commits to its predecessor, and the actor and any DID-shaped target are committed under a keyed hash **with the plaintext beside them** — so an erasure nulls the plaintext, the row stays correlatable, and the chain digest (which excludes the plaintext members) still verifies.

**The chain opens with the creation of the key that chains it** — your design. The key is established on the first write, because there is nothing to audit before a node can act and a node cannot act before it has somewhere to record what it did. So the first entry is the record of that key coming into existence, committing to its id: a verifier reading from the start learns which key the following entries are hashed under, from an entry hashed under that same key.

A DID-shaped resource becomes the hashed target; anything else — a key id, a session id, a context path — is not personal data and stays in the event.

## The bug the tests found

The storage key needed a **nanosecond tiebreaker**, and the reason is worth recording.

Whole seconds put two entries written in the same second into *uuid order*. A verifier reading the log in key order then sees them out of chain order and **reports a break in a chain that is intact** — a false alarm indistinguishable from the thing the chain exists to detect. Review would not have caught it; three tests failed with `BrokenLink { index: 0 }` and that is what it turned out to be.

The seconds stay the **leading** field, because `cleanup_expired_logs` compares keys against `log:{cutoff:020}:` and stops at the first row past it. A different leading field would make every chained row sort past every cutoff and never expire.

## The read path

`audit/list` now accepts both shapes. This is why the two halves could not be split: a reader that knows only one shape **does not fail loudly** — it logs "skipping unparseable audit row" and moves on — so shipping the sink alone would have produced a log that silently appears to stop at the moment chaining began.

## Tests

Four on the sink: the chain opens with its own key's creation; writes chain to one another and `verify_chain` passes; a second sink over the same keyspace continues the chain rather than opening a second one (the restart path); and a DID resource becomes a hashed target while a key id does not.

## Still open

Retention versus the chain — deleting the tail leaves the remainder unverifiable, which the note covers and the checkpoint mechanism answers. And the `verify` surface: chaining nobody can check is a hash column, not tamper-evidence.

title: feat(audit): give the VTA an audit key of its own
body:
Next step of the audit-chaining work ([#1415](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1415) settled the design). Two pieces, both inert until the sink uses them.

## `ensure_initial_random`

Establishes an initial key from the OS random source rather than from a seed, idempotently, so a node can call it on every start.

The reasoning, per #1415: the key's job is to be a **stable handle** for actor and target identifiers — exist before the first write, stay retrievable while any envelope references it, be rotatable. Nothing about that requires it to be derivable.

What derivation *adds* is a second copy of the key wherever the seed is. A node whose recovery story is a mnemonic therefore has an audit key that anyone holding the mnemonic can recompute — and since the commitment exists precisely so an erasure can null the plaintext while the row stays correlatable, **that makes the erasure reversible by brute force** over the identifiers the node has seen.

Two tests: a generated key is established once and returned unchanged after; and it is not reproducible from the seed, nor from another generated key.

## The keyspace

`audit_key`, registered in `ALL` and in the **backed-up** set.

Backed up because the key is not regenerable — that is the cost of generating rather than deriving. Without it a restored audit log still verifies as a chain and still says what happened, but no entry can be checked against a candidate identifier again: the commitments become opaque.

Separate from `audit` because the two have **opposite lifetimes**: entries are erased when their retention expires, and a key must outlive every entry that references it. Neither cascades on a DID deletion, for the reason the audit log already does not — the record that a DID was deleted is the one thing that must survive deleting it.

## Next

The sink. It ensures the key on first write — which is what makes the genesis entry work: the first entry in the chain is the creation of the key that chains it, written by the same call that creates it.

title: Record what the divergence register has moved
body:
Appendix F, updated from implementation work against its entries. Three change state, one closes.

## One closes

**VTI-SES-006 / VTI-SES-007** — the challenge operation now answers every caller identically and persists a session only for an enrolled subject, moving the refusal to authentication, which requires the subject's private key. Every failure reachable *without* that key renders one message, so the disclosure does not reappear at the other end of the flow.

A closed entry leaves the tables, per F.6's rule, and is listed in a new **F.5 Closed** — so a reader can tell a register that is being worked from one that has been abandoned. That distinction is the whole value of the artefact.

## One records the resolution taken

**VTI-VTA-004 / VTI-VTA-005** — **domain separation**, chosen over parsing what is presented. The entry now records what that means: the externally reachable path frames its payload under a versioned tag before signing, so the signature verifies as a payload of that operation and nothing else.

And the part that only shows up when you build it: **the in-process proof constructor is excluded by name.** Its bytes carry a meaning its own specification established, including how a verifier reconstructs them, so framing them again produces a proof a conforming verifier rejects. That is why the domain is an argument every call site states rather than a prefix applied to all of them — a distinction the resolution column previously did not have, because nobody had tried it yet.

## Two record what preparing the work settled

**VTI-AUD-004** — chain by default, reusing the scheme the other node type already runs rather than adding a second. Settled while preparing it: **the chain's first entry is the creation of the key that chains it**, so a verifier reading from the start learns which key the following entries are hashed under from an entry hashed under that same key. Rotation takes the same shape, each key's segment opening with the record of why the key changed.

**VTI-AUD-005** — commit to the identifier under a keyed hash and keep the plaintext beside it: an erasure nulls the plaintext, the commitment keeps the row correlatable, and the chain digest excludes the plaintext members so it still verifies.

**The key is randomly generated rather than derived from the master seed.** Derivation would make the recovery phrase an audit-key backup, so an erasure would be reversible by brute force — over the small candidate space of identifiers that node has seen — for anyone holding it. Still the entry most worth resolving before a deployment carries personal data at scale, because it cannot be fixed retroactively for records already written.

states rather than a prefix applied to all of them.

reuses the scheme another node type already runs; its first entry is
the creation of the key that chains it, and rotation takes the same

title: feat(room-host): actually serve the identity the VTA holds
body:
`fetch_identity` was written, documented and referenced by its own module docs —
and called by nothing. Across the whole workspace it had two references: its
definition, and a doc comment pointing at it.

So `--vta-did` did exactly one thing: mint a throwaway, print the grant, and on
the next start report "enrolled with the VTA". The host then served under the
`did:peer:2` it minted for `--mediator-did`, and the ACL grant bought nothing.
Every log line said the VTA-governed path was working. Nothing in it ran.

This is the same shape as the `rematerialise`-called-from-nowhere defect: code
that reads as a live feature because it is complete, tested at the edges, and
unreachable.

## The wiring

- `HostIdentity::from_vta` — the VTA's DID and the keys published under it, used
  verbatim. Deliberately not sharing a path with `load_or_mint`: that one mints,
  checks the identifier encodes the right mediator, and writes an identity file,
  and none of those are right for a DID somebody else published. A `did:webvh`
  carries a service block rather than an encoded mediator, and second-guessing
  it would be this host arguing with the party that issued its identity.
- `--vta-context`, defaulting to `rooms`. `fetch_identity` always needed one and
  there was no flag to supply it, which is its own evidence the call site never
  existed.
- **Enrolment moved before the identity is chosen.** It can `return`, and
  minting a `did:peer` first left one in the data directory that the governed
  path would never use.
- One secrets store, hoisted, shared by the cached VTA identity and the
  self-minted one — so `--secrets` covers both and an operator configures where
  key material rests once.

An unreachable VTA is not fatal: the host comes up on the cached identity and
warns. Losing every host when the VTA blinks is a far larger blast radius than
the outage, for a process that only stores ciphertext.

## A feature that never compiled

`--features onboarding` alone failed with four errors on `main` and always has:
`onboarding.rs` returns `Vec<Secret>` from `affinidi-secrets-resolver`, which
only `didcomm` pulled in. Every build that had both hid it. Fixed by declaring
what the feature actually needs, and all four combinations now build — none,
`didcomm`, `onboarding`, both.

That is a small thing that says something: the feature meant to be the VTA path
had never been built on its own, which is consistent with the call site never
having been written.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: security(keys)!: domain-separate the opaque signing oracle
body:
Implements the option you chose for **VTI-VTA-004** — the blind-signing finding from the [specification](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-vti-spec/) gap analysis.

## The problem

`keys/sign` signs an octet string the caller supplies, under a key the caller names. The authorization around it is genuinely good — context, the context's `signable_keys` policy, the entry's own key narrowing, super-admin-only for unscoped keys — but **all of it bounds *which key* signs, and none of it bounds *what the bytes mean***.

So a caller authorized to sign for one purpose could obtain a signature that verifies as something else entirely: an assertion in another protocol, a token, a proof over a document the principal never saw. The type's own doc said as much — *"the VTA signs the bytes it is given without inspecting them"* — and treated it as a caller-side concern.

## The fix

Payloads the VTA cannot parse are framed under `vti.vta.opaque-signing.v1` before signing, so the signature verifies as **a VTA opaque-signing payload and as nothing else**.

This does not make signing arbitrary bytes safe. It makes the result unusable outside the domain it was requested in, which is what domain separation buys and the limit of what it buys.

## Why it is an argument, not a blanket prefix

**One caller must not be framed.** `room_issuance.rs` signs data-integrity proof inputs through this same function — bytes whose meaning the proof specification has already established, including how a verifier reconstructs them. Framing those again produces a proof that a conforming verifier rejects.

So `SigningDomain` is an explicit argument and every call site states which case it is in:

- `Opaque` — REST, DIDComm and the Trust Task, where the payload came from a caller;
- `ProtocolDefined` — the in-process proof signer, where the caller is the code that built the bytes.

They are not interchangeable, and the enum's docs say why at each variant.

## Breaking change

Signatures over `keys/sign` now cover the framed input rather than the payload as supplied. **A verifier reconstructs it with `opaque_signing_input`**, published in the SDK for exactly that. Signatures made before this change do not verify against the new input, and vice versa — there is no compatibility mode, because one would reintroduce the property being removed.

Proofs built inside the VTA are unaffected.

## Tests

Five, on the framing itself: an opaque payload is not signed as presented; protocol-defined bytes are; the two domains never agree on the bytes — including for a payload that *starts with the tag*; the framing cannot be pre-applied by a chosen payload (the tag carries no NUL, so the first NUL is always the separator); and a verifier can reconstruct what was signed.

title: docs: record where the VTA's audit key should come from
body:
Stacked on #1413. One section in the audit-chaining note, replacing stage 1's assumption that the VTA derives its audit key from the master seed "mirroring the VTC".

**A correction first.** The first version of this PR claimed a VTA *cannot* derive the key at boot, because a sealed VTA has no seed until an operator unseals. That was wrong: the seal is an **offline-CLI guard** that refuses state-mutating commands, enforced in `main.rs`, not a runtime secret lock — and the server reaches the seed store during boot already. Thanks to @glenngore for the question that prompted the check.

The real question turns out to be about privacy, not availability.

## Derive, or generate?

The audit key's job is to be a stable HMAC handle for actor and target identifiers: it must exist before the first write, stay retrievable while any envelope references it, and be rotatable. **It does not need to be derivable from anything**, and the key store already stores, rotates and keeps history.

| | Derived from the seed | Randomly generated |
|---|---|---|
| Availability at first write | Depends on the seed store answering — for a cloud secret manager or Vault that is a network call that can fail at boot, and the VTC's answer to that failure is an `Option<AuditWriter>` falling back to unchained rows | Available from first boot, no dependency to fail |
| Recovery if the `audit_key` keyspace is lost | Regenerable from the mnemonic — matters if envelopes were shipped off-node to a SIEM and only the local key store was lost | Gone. Mitigated by keeping `audit_key` in the backup set, leaving the gap at "backups lost, mnemonic survives" |
| **Who can recompute an actor hash** | **Anyone holding the mnemonic, forever** | Whoever holds the key material |

**The third row decides it.** VTI-AUD-005 exists so an erasure removes personal data while the record stays verifiable. Deriving the audit key from the master seed makes the mnemonic an audit-key backup — so the erasure is undone by whoever holds the recovery phrase, by brute force over a small candidate space (the identifiers this node has seen). For a stack whose recovery story *is* the mnemonic, that is a wide set.

So: **random, for the VTA.**

This makes the VTA's key source differ from the VTC's. That is deliberate rather than inconsistent — and the same reasoning applies to a VTC, whose rotation machinery is the path if the working group wants to move it.

## What it needs

`ensure_initial_random` beside the `ensure_initial_with_info` added in #1412, and `audit_key` in the VTA's backed-up keyspaces.

title: docs: record where the VTA's audit key should come from (#1415)
body:
docs: record where the VTA's audit key should come from (#1415)

* docs: correct the audit-key source section

An earlier revision of this commit claimed a VTA cannot derive the
audit key at boot because a sealed VTA has no master seed until an
operator unseals. That is wrong. The seal is an offline-CLI guard that
refuses state-mutating commands; it is enforced in main.rs, not in the
server, and the server reaches the seed store during boot already.

The question the mistake was circling is real but different, and it is
about privacy rather than availability. Deriving the audit key from the
master seed makes the mnemonic an audit-key backup, so an erasure that
nulls an actor's plaintext is reversible by brute force for whoever
holds the recovery phrase — over a candidate space of the identifiers
this node has seen. A randomly generated key confines that to whoever
holds the key material, needs no seed to exist before the first write,
and fits the key store's existing rotation and history.

The note now records that comparison and what it needs: an
ensure_initial_random beside ensure_initial_with_info, and audit_key in
the backed-up keyspaces.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs: the first audit entry is the creation of its own key

There is no window before the key exists that needs auditing, because
there is nothing a VTA can do before its seed is loaded: no keys, no
signing, no ACL to consult, no context to act in. Checked rather than
assumed — the setup path emits no audit call before the seed record is
saved, and boot emits none before the seed is available.

So the first entry in the chain is the creation of the key that chains
it, written the moment that key exists and committing to its id. A
verifier reading from the start learns which key the following entries
are hashed under, from an entry hashed under that same key. Rotation
takes the same shape: the first entry of a new key's era records why
the key changed.

The one event that stays outside the chain is a failure to obtain the
seed at all, which cannot be chained because the key that would chain
it does not exist. That is acceptable exactly there: a node that cannot
load its seed is not serving.

title: feat(audit): let the writer serve a keyspace that predates chaining
body:
Stacked on #1412. Two changes to `AuditWriter`, both prerequisites for the VTA using it, neither altering VTC behaviour.

Found by trying to point the writer at a VTA's audit keyspace and reading what would happen.

## The storage key becomes configurable

A keyspace that already holds rows has an **ordering**, and a writer that ignores it produces a log whose newest entry is not its last key — which breaks chain-head recovery *and* every reader that pages in key order.

A VTA's audit keyspace is exactly that keyspace: it holds `log:<zero-padded-epoch>:<uuid>` rows, and those sort **after** an RFC 3339 timestamp. So a VTA supplies its own key function and its ordering stays uniform. `envelope_storage_key` remains the default; a fresh keyspace needs nothing.

## Chain-head recovery tolerates rows that predate the chain

`load_chain_head` read the last key in ascending order and deserialized it as an envelope. Against a VTA that row is a pre-chain row, so **the first chained write would fail** — not because anything is wrong, but because the row beside it was written before the scheme existed.

It now walks back to the newest row that *is* an envelope, and anchors at genesis if there is none. Deserialization is the test rather than the key, because the key format now belongs to the caller: a value either is an envelope or is not.

## Tests

- `a_pre_chain_row_does_not_break_the_first_write` — seeds a row in the exact shape and key format a VTA wrote before chaining, then asserts the first chained write succeeds and anchors at genesis.
- `a_custom_storage_key_still_recovers_the_head` — writes under a VTA-shaped key, then builds a *fresh* writer over the same keyspace (the path a restart takes) and asserts the second entry chains to the first and the pair verifies.

92 audit tests pass in `vti-common`.

## Next

The VTA side: `audit_key` keyspace and key store at boot, the sink writing envelopes through this writer under the `log:` key format, and the read path accepting both values. Those land together — the read path is what keeps `audit/list` working across the switch.

title: refactor(audit): one construction point for the audit sink, and the prerequisites for chaining it
body:
Two commits, both aimed at the same follow-up: giving the VTA the tamper-evident audit log the VTC already has ([#1408](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1408), as corrected by [#1410](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1410)). Neither changes behaviour.

## 1. One construction point

The workspace built the same sink over the same keyspace in **thirty-one places** — including **three times inside one function**, `run_create_did_webvh`, which already had one in scope two hundred lines above the other two. Every one of those was somewhere a later change to what a VTA's audit writes would have to be found and repeated.

There is now one constructor, `vta_audit::shared_keyspace_sink`, and every caller goes through it. A server still takes its sink from `AppState` — that path was already right, and its comment already explained why ("built once here and handed to *both* the storage thread and `AppStateParts`"). The factory is for callers with **no `AppState` to take one from**: offline CLI commands, setup, sweepers and tests.

29 call sites now use it; the three inside `run_create_did_webvh` became one.

## 2. Prerequisites for chaining

**`AuditEvent::VtaOperation`.** Every other variant names one thing that can happen to a community, because a VTC's audit surface is a closed set of community events. A VTA's is not: it audits every gated operation it serves, the set grows with the task catalogue, and its call sites already carry a dotted action name rather than a type. Modelling each as a variant would mean an enum that changes whenever an operation does, and a wire contract that breaks with it. So the action stays a string and the variant carries the four things a VTA call site supplies beside it — while the actor and any DID-shaped target travel in the envelope's hashed members, where an erasure can reach them.

**`AuditKeyStore::ensure_initial_with_info`**, plus named constants for the two info strings in use. The default derivation is unchanged, so an existing community's hashes stay verifiable — a test pins that.

The reason for the parameter is worth stating: **a VTC is provisioned on top of a VTA and can reach the same master seed.** Deriving both logs' keys under one label would give two different audit logs one HMAC key, so an actor hash would correlate across them — which is precisely the correlation the hash exists to contain. Three tests cover it: different keys per node type from one seed, the unchanged default, and derivation being idempotent across boots.

## What comes next

Slice B — the sink writes envelopes through `AuditWriter` and the read path handles both forms. Those must land together: the storage key and the value both change, so the existing `audit/list` query stops finding rows it can parse. Slice C adds `verify`. Retention still needs the checkpoint work, per the note.

title: vta-service-v0.25.1
body:
### Added

- **persona**: Say whether a link crosses a part of the holder's life ([#1342](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1342))

Serves the members added in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#408, published in
  trust-tasks-rs 0.18.10: `crossesFacets` and `facetIds` on a finding,
  `facetId` on each `sharedWith` location. This needs a floor of 0.18.10 —
  the spine validates OUTGOING responses, so under an older schema an analysis
  that fully succeeded would come back 500 `responseSchemaViolation` — and no
  longer moves one: main reached 0.18.11 while this sat open, which satisfies
  it. The bump this branch carried is dropped rather than resolved downward.

  **Severity is how linkable. Facets are whether the holder minds.** Nothing
  here touches `severity`, and that is the design rather than an omission. A
  value shared between two profiles in one facet still links them for anyone
  who sees both — the holder's filing changes nothing a counterparty can do —
  so softening severity on intent would report a false all-clear. What the
  facets add is a second axis: which of these findings the holder would
  actually want to act on.

  **Absent is unknown, not false.** `crosses_facets` is `Option<bool>` and is
  `None` when the holder keeps no facets, because `false` asserts these
  identities sit in one part of a life and an agent with no facets has made no
  such finding. `FacetIndex::any` is what carries that distinction, which is
  why the index is a struct rather than a map.

  **An unarranged profile is not a second facet.** Only distinct, named facets
  count toward a crossing. Counting "no facet" as one would make every holder
  who has arranged one part of their life and not the rest see a crossing on
  everything they own — the dismissal problem arriving from the other
  direction.

  `facet_index` is built once per analysis for the reason `disclosure_index`
  is: `analyze_correlation` with no `attributeId` walks the whole pool, and
  the per-finding shape re-lists every facet for every finding.

  The conformance witness now exercises the three new members rather than
  merely permitting them — they are the ones added last, and an outgoing
  member the embedded schema has not caught up with is a 500 on a call that
  succeeded.

  vta-persona 118/118 (6 new, one per rule above), vta-service lib 1063/1063,
  clippy --all-targets clean.

- **rooms**: Cut over to present/0.2 and issue-authority/0.2 ([#1365](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1365))

The consuming half of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#415 and #418, unblocked
  by affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#784.

  `trust-tasks-rs` 0.19 carries both new spec versions, but this workspace could
  not take it: `affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.22.0` required 0.18, so pinning 0.19 put
  two `trust-tasks-rs` nodes in the graph and broke `vta-sdk` on `expected
  MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`. TDK #784 moved the messaging family
  to 0.19 and 0.23.0.

  Taking it exposed pins that had drifted apart underneath: `vta-sdk` was on
  messaging-sdk 0.22 while `vta-service` and the e2e tests were on 0.21, and three
  `trust-tasks-rs` versions were resolving at once. All of it is now consolidated:
  the lockfile holds exactly ONE `trust-tasks-rs` and ONE `affinidi-messaging-sdk`,
  where before it held three of each.

  `rooms/keys/present` 0.1 -> 0.2 and `rooms/owner/issue-authority` 0.1 -> 0.2.
  Both 0.1s are retired upstream. Neither is dual-accepted, deliberately: for
  `present`, 0.1's extra members are exactly the two nothing could honour; for
  `issue-authority`, accepting 0.1 means accepting a request with no `validUntil`,
  which is the thing 0.2 exists to refuse.

  The hand-rolled `validUntil` guard in `room_owner.rs` is deleted. 0.2 makes the
  member REQUIRED, so the generated payload types it as a `DateTime` and the
  envelope schema rejects a request without one before dispatch. Same rule, one
  layer up, which is where a shape constraint belongs.

  `every_witnessed_task_round_trips_through_its_generated_types` refused two
  witnesses that had been green for as long as they existed:

  1. The `issue-authority` witness carried no `validUntil` — a chain root with no
     expiry, the exact request 0.2 forbids, and one this service could have sent.
  2. The `present` witness carried `"audience": "did:key:z6MkHost"` — a HOST DID,
     the precise shape #414 reported as impossible to satisfy, since the field
     named the party that had to PRESENT the credential.

  `room_oracle` emitted `membership` and `authority[]` as JSON **objects**;
  `AuthorityPresentation` types both as strings, and the host's opener reads
  base64url or bare JSON text. So the oracle's output could not deserialize at a
  host at all — `rooms/keys/present` had never worked end to end. It went unseen
  because 0.1's response typed `presentation` as an opaque object; 0.2 names the
  shared component, which turned a runtime refusal nothing exercised into a type
  error. The oracle now serialises each credential. That is the first half of
  have caught all three of these years earlier.

* feat(rooms): a `host` feature, so a room's member half reaches wasm

  `vti-rooms` already had two halves and no name for them: `vta-service`
  imports `mls`/`sealed`/`wire` and nothing else, while `vtc-service`,
  `room-host` and `vti-rooms-dtg` import `storage`/`authz`/`audit`. This
  names the second half `host`, on by default, and makes `vti-common`
  optional behind it.

  `vti-common` describes itself as server-side infrastructure and pulls
  axum, fjall and tokio, so it was the whole of what kept a room's member
  code off `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. With it optional,
  `--no-default-features --features mls` builds there — which is what lets
  a browser hold a room's keys itself rather than ask an agent to. See
  `docs/05-design-notes/data-rooms-demo-site.md`.

  The member half needed **no source changes** to get there. That is a
  property of `error.rs`, which deliberately does not use
  `vti_common::error::AppError` because key material is not a service's
  concern; a decision made for its own reasons that paid for itself here.

  `lifecycle` is deliberately left ungated: only hosts consume it today,
  but it needs nothing from `vti-common`, and a member computing a room's
  lifecycle state to explain it on screen should not need a host's
  dependencies.

  Three things about the wasm plumbing, each of which reports as a
  `compile_error!` that reads like an unsupported target:

  - OpenMLS 0.9 has a first-class `js` feature (`web-time` for the
    `SystemTime` wasm lacks, plus getrandom's JS backend). Declared
    per-target rather than as a feature of this crate, so building for
    wasm just works — verified wasm-only: `web-time` appears in the wasm
    tree and not the native one.
  - There are two getrandom majors in the graph. The 0.4 is ours; the 0.2
    arrives transitively under `openmls_rust_crypto` via RustCrypto's
    elliptic-curve stack, so no feature declared here could reach it.
    `getrandom_02` is a feature shim, not a dependency this crate calls.
  - With both declared per-target, **no `RUSTFLAGS` are needed** — the
    `wasm_js` feature alone selects the backend.

  no host, and a wasm32 `--lib` check, so neither property rots silently.

  `vta-service` now takes `default-features = false`: a VTA holds room keys
  and is never a room's host, so it no longer compiles one.

  WebAssembly, so a tab can *be* a member rather than drive an agent that
  is one. `vti-rooms` supplies all of it; this crate is only the boundary,
  and its job is deciding what crosses.

  ciphertext, an epoch number — with one deliberate exception: the
  snapshot, which is key material because OpenMLS persists a group through
  its provider rather than as a value. It goes in IndexedDB and nowhere

title: vta-persona-v0.3.2
body:
### Added

- **persona**: Say whether a link crosses a part of the holder's life ([#1342](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1342))

Serves the members added in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#408, published in
  trust-tasks-rs 0.18.10: `crossesFacets` and `facetIds` on a finding,
  `facetId` on each `sharedWith` location. This needs a floor of 0.18.10 —
  the spine validates OUTGOING responses, so under an older schema an analysis
  that fully succeeded would come back 500 `responseSchemaViolation` — and no
  longer moves one: main reached 0.18.11 while this sat open, which satisfies
  it. The bump this branch carried is dropped rather than resolved downward.

  **Severity is how linkable. Facets are whether the holder minds.** Nothing
  here touches `severity`, and that is the design rather than an omission. A
  value shared between two profiles in one facet still links them for anyone
  who sees both — the holder's filing changes nothing a counterparty can do —
  so softening severity on intent would report a false all-clear. What the
  facets add is a second axis: which of these findings the holder would
  actually want to act on.

  **Absent is unknown, not false.** `crosses_facets` is `Option<bool>` and is
  `None` when the holder keeps no facets, because `false` asserts these
  identities sit in one part of a life and an agent with no facets has made no
  such finding. `FacetIndex::any` is what carries that distinction, which is
  why the index is a struct rather than a map.

  **An unarranged profile is not a second facet.** Only distinct, named facets
  count toward a crossing. Counting "no facet" as one would make every holder
  who has arranged one part of their life and not the rest see a crossing on
  everything they own — the dismissal problem arriving from the other
  direction.

  `facet_index` is built once per analysis for the reason `disclosure_index`
  is: `analyze_correlation` with no `attributeId` walks the whole pool, and
  the per-finding shape re-lists every facet for every finding.

  The conformance witness now exercises the three new members rather than
  merely permitting them — they are the ones added last, and an outgoing
  member the embedded schema has not caught up with is a 500 on a call that
  succeeded.

  vta-persona 118/118 (6 new, one per rule above), vta-service lib 1063/1063,
  clippy --all-targets clean.

- **persona**: Serve persona/facet — the holder's arrangement of their identity ([#1338](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1338))

Implements the three tasks specified in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#405, published
  in trust-tasks-rs 0.18.9.

  A holder who uses this model for a while ends up with twenty profiles, and a
  flat list of twenty is a list nobody reads. A facet is the arrangement over
  them — "Work", "Home", "Play" — and it is agent-scoped, like the pool and
  the profiles it groups.

  **An arrangement, not a container.** Nothing is stored inside a facet, and
  `delete_facet` touches no profile and no attribute. There is no cascading
  form because there is no cascading form of the idea: a grouping that could
  take its members with it is a folder, and a holder who reads it as a folder
  is right to be afraid of it. `releasedFaces` reports what now belongs
  nowhere, which is what a screen needs to say what it will look like
  afterwards. `deleting_a_facet_deletes_nothing_it_named` pins it.

  **Membership lives on the facet.** A `facet_id` on `Attribute` would be the
  obvious alternative and is the wrong shape: `attribute/put` REPLACES, and a
  well-behaved consumer does not hold the values it would have to resend —
  `attribute/list` withholds `sensitivity: high` plaintext unless asked by
  name. It would either request every sensitive value the holder owns to
  perform an arrangement that has nothing to do with values, or send a put
  without one and destroy them.

title: vti-rooms-dtg-v0.2.1
body:
### Fixed

- **rooms**: A presentation is bound to its presenter — and dtg-credentials 0.6 → 0.9.1 ([#1356](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1356))

* fix(rooms): bind a presentation to its presenter, not to the host

  `pnm-cli rooms --host-did …` could never work. Every request it made was
  refused as `WrongAudience`, and omitting the flag "worked" only by
  skipping the check it exists to perform — so the flag's two states were
  broken and unprotected.

  `audience` is not who a presentation is addressed to.
  `dtg_credentials::authority::verify_chain` compares it to the PRESENTER —
  "the leaf must be presentable by whoever is presenting it" — so it is
  holder binding, and its whole job is to make a captured presentation
  worthless to whoever captured it. Filled with the host's DID it named a
  party no presenter can ever match.

  The value to bind to was already named a few lines away: `RoomSigner`'s
  doc says "a room request is signed by the party the presentation was
  minted for". This passes exactly that. There is no unbound case left, so
  the warning about one goes, and `--host-did` keeps its real job of naming
  the document's recipient.

body:
### Added

- **rooms**: Traces, and a response type for the single-record read ([#1368](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1368))

A commitment lets a reader catch a host that equivocates. A trace proves a
  particular record sits under the root that host just asserted. This serves
  them — and fixes the conformance defect that adding them uncovered.

  Implements trust-tasks-tf#419, released as trust-tasks-rs 0.19.1.

  `rooms/records/get` has never conformed to its published schema. Both hosts
  answered a read by serialising `vti_rooms::Record` — the *storage* record — and
  adding `dataCommitment` to whatever came out:

      "c2VhbGVk" is not of type "object";
      Additional properties are not allowed
      ('author','epoch','nonce','pinned','status','updatedAt' were unexpected)

  It survived because `vti_rooms::wire`'s rule — every wire type appears in
  tests/schema_conformance.rs — can only be applied to types that exist. A
  response that was never a type had no line to be missing from, and a storage
  record reached the wire because nothing stood between them. The consumer is not
  hypothetical: `@openvtc/pnm-core`'s `roomsRecordsGet` is typed on the generated
  payload, so a caller reading `sealed.ciphertext` got `undefined` from a live
  host, with a green type-check on both sides.

  The leaf preimage was not reproducible either. `leaf_hash` canonicalised the
  storage record, so every root it produced was unreachable by any reader:
  `updatedAt` is unix seconds in storage and RFC 3339 on the wire, `epoch` and
  `nonce` are flat in storage and inside `sealed` on the wire, and `epoch`
  serialises as `null` on an open room where the wire has it absent. Survivable
  while the only use was comparing two roots from the same build; not survivable
  once a trace has to be computable by someone else.

- **rooms**: Hosts compute and serve the data commitment ([#1351](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1351))

* fix(rooms): a commitment is a DigestMultibase, not bare hex

  Owed from #1346. The spec that landed with it
  (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#411) types `dataCommitment` as the
  framework's `DigestMultibase`, and the helper shipped emitting hex.

  Bare hex hard-codes SHA-256 into the wire contract, which is precisely what
  `DigestMultibase` exists to prevent: multihash names the algorithm in-band,
  so moving off SHA-256 later is a change of value rather than another schema
  revision. `0x12 0x20` then the digest, base58btc with the `z` prefix — the
  same shape `sealed_transfer::bundle_digest_multibase` already produces, so
  the two agree by construction rather than by memory.

  `from_multibase` refuses anything that is not a sha2-256 multihash. A
  commitment is what a comparison turns on, so silently accepting an algorithm
  this build cannot compute would turn "these two roots differ" into "these
  two roots are not comparable" without saying which.

  Two tests, both about the encoding being a contract rather than a detail: a
  commitment decodes to the 34-byte multihash and round-trips, and bare hex, a
  foreign algorithm, a truncated digest and non-multibase are each refused.

  The tree, the leaves and the proofs are untouched — this is the wire
  boundary only.

- **rooms**: A browser can be a room member ([#1347](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1347))

  `vti-rooms` already had two halves and no name for them: `vta-service`

  names the second half `host`, on by default, and makes `vti-common`
  optional behind it.

  `vti-common` describes itself as server-side infrastructure and pulls
  axum, fjall and tokio, so it was the whole of what kept a room's member
  code off `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. With it optional,
  `--no-default-features --features mls` builds there — which is what lets
  a browser hold a room's keys itself rather than ask an agent to. See
  `docs/05-design-notes/data-rooms-demo-site.md`.

  The member half needed **no source changes** to get there. That is a
  property of `error.rs`, which deliberately does not use
  `vti_common::error::AppError` because key material is not a service's
  concern; a decision made for its own reasons that paid for itself here.

  `lifecycle` is deliberately left ungated: only hosts consume it today,
  but it needs nothing from `vti-common`, and a member computing a room's
  lifecycle state to explain it on screen should not need a host's
  dependencies.

  `compile_error!` that reads like an unsupported target:

  - OpenMLS 0.9 has a first-class `js` feature (`web-time` for the

    per-target rather than as a feature of this crate, so building for
    wasm just works — verified wasm-only: `web-time` appears in the wasm
    tree and not the native one.

    arrives transitively under `openmls_rust_crypto` via RustCrypto's

    `getrandom_02` is a feature shim, not a dependency this crate calls.
  - With both declared per-target, **no `RUSTFLAGS` are needed** — the
    `wasm_js` feature alone selects the backend.

  CI gains two steps in the `features` job: clippy on the member half with
  no host, and a wasm32 `--lib` check, so neither property rots silently.

  `vta-service` now takes `default-features = false`: a VTA holds room keys
  and is never a room's host, so it no longer compiles one.
